arXiv:2504.02448v1 [cs.DC] 03 Apr 2025

Towards Learning-Augmented Peer-to-Peer Networks: Self-Stabilizing Graph Linearization with Untrusted Advice

Vijeth Aradhya ††thanks: National University of Singapore, Singapore.    Christian Scheideler ††thanks: Paderborn University, Germany.
Abstract

Distributed peer-to-peer systems are widely popular due to their decentralized nature, which ensures that no peer is critical for the functionality of the system. However, fully decentralized solutions are usually much harder to design, and tend to have a much higher overhead compared to centralized approaches, where the peers are connected to a powerful server. On the other hand, centralized approaches have a single point of failure. Thus, is there some way to combine their advantages without inheriting their disadvantages? To that end, we consider a supervised peer-to-peer approach where the peers can ask a potentially unreliable supervisor for advice. This is in line with the increasingly popular algorithmic paradigm called algorithms with predictions or learning-augmented algorithms, but we are the first to consider it in the context of peer-to-peer networks.

Specifically, we design self-stabilizing algorithms for the fundamental problem of distributed graph linearization, where peers are supposed to recover the “sorted line” network from any initial network after a transient fault. With the help of the supervisor, peers can recover the sorted line network in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) time, if the advice is correct; otherwise, the algorithm retains its original recovery time (i.e., without any supervisor). A crucial challenge that we overcome is to correctly compose multiple self-stabilizing algorithms, that is, one that processes and exploits the advice, and another that does not rely on the advice at all. Our key technical contributions combine ideas from the fields of overlay networks and proof-labeling schemes. Finally, we give a matching lower bound of Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) for the recovery time of any algorithm if the advice can be corrupted, where nn is the network size.

Keywords: distributed algorithms, overlay networks, self-stabilization, proof-labeling schemes

1 Introduction

Traditionally, online algorithms augmented with advice is an area of research where one attempts to measure how much knowledge of the future is necessary to achieve a given competitive ratio [27, 15]. However, the advice might not always be helpful since it is usually hard to predict the future sufficiently well. Ideally, we would like that bad advice does not result in a competitive ratio that is worse than what is achieved without any advice. Motivated by recent advances in machine learning, a new line of research has thus looked at algorithms with predictions [65]. In this framework [64], the algorithm takes advantage of an extra piece of information, called “prediction” (also called “advice” or “hint”), to achieve (near) optimal performance if the prediction is good, while also not performing (much) worse than an algorithm without prediction, if the prediction is bad.

While competitive analysis in the sequential online setting has been predominant for modeling temporal uncertainty (i.e., the input is arriving piece by piece, and decisions need to be made on the fly), problems in distributed networks typically arise from spatial uncertainty where the input itself is divided among several compute nodes, and all nodes collectively perform global computation [69, 42, 75, 4]. To surmount the uncertainty, many researchers have investigated trade-offs between the size of advice and the network’s performance for many problems (e.g., [37, 32, 33, 34, 51, 26]), seeking to minimize the information needed to efficiently solve them. Recently, however, there has been a growing trend towards designing distributed algorithms that can not only exploit the advice for better performance, but are also robust (i.e., retain their native performance without any advice) when the advice is unreliable [38, 41, 1, 14].

We initiate the study of algorithms with untrusted advice for peer-to-peer systems, where the peers continuously execute local algorithms to maintain a desirable network with certain connectivity properties. As these systems are highly dynamic (for e.g., due to churn, link failures, memory corruption, etc), such algorithms should quickly recover the network after any failure. To that end, we consider the self-stabilization framework [21] that requires the system to converge to a desirable state after any transient fault which can arbitrarily corrupt the system state. Following the pioneering work of Dijkstra [21], self-stabilization has been promising for modeling recovery in distributed systems (e.g., [8, 24, 17, 60, 43, 13, 16]); for books, see [22, 76].

Specifically, we consider a network model where there is a supervisor that can be contacted by the peers if they need advice. Supervised networks have been considered in the past (e.g., [53, 35, 29, 2]), but there only the case has been studied that the advice is reliable. In that scenario, the peers can trust all the connections suggested by the supervisor, which would make the self-stabilization problem for overlay networks very easy: simply suggest the set of peers some peer should ideally be connected to. But if the advice can be corrupted, for example, an advice to connect to non-existing peers, then a malicious supervisor could easily start so-called Sybil attacks [25], i.e., attacks integrating many potentially malicious peers into the peer-to-peer (P2P) system, that were previously not part of it.

To prevent such attacks, the advice of the supervisor must be limited to peers that a peer is already connected to. Indeed, this scenario has been recently considered in [72], but that work only considered how quickly a well-behaved supervisor can compute a near-optimal schedule for transforming any initial overlay network into the desired overlay network, given that it can only suggest network transformations by pointing to connections that the peers currently have. Bad advice can be hard for peers to identify since they are only aware of their local neighborhood. It is crucial that the advice does not throw the stabilization process backwards so that the peers never converge to the desired network. Further, a crucial challenge is that self-stabilizing algorithms must converge from any initial state, including arbitrarily bad advice from the supervisor.

Despite the obstacles, we develop a generic self-stabilizing mechanism for solving the fundamental problem of distributed graph linearization (topological sorting) [67, 45, 66, 36, 73], where each peer connects to its adjacent peer(s) in the topological sorted order to form the so-called sorted line network, no matter what kind of advice is given. This is achieved by a modular design of separately executing lightweight self-stabilizing algorithms that process the advice, and any self-stabilizing algorithm that converges to the sorted line network without any advice.

Our advice messages are of small size (per peer), and enable the peers to quickly build a hypercubic structure that facilitates efficient information exchange. Using that structure, a peer is able to connect to any other peer in the network. Crucially, the advice is also verifiable in the sense that if the advice is bad, the peers can quickly detect it and stop making any additional connections due to that advice. Indeed, an added advantage of being able to detect bad advice in the self-stabilization setting is that the peers can quickly return to a state where they are again ready to receive (correct) advice from the supervisor.

Organization.   First, we describe our contributions, related work, and model. In Section 2, we state a few preliminaries. In Section 3, we describe all the different aspects of the advice. In Section 4, we provide the key details of the self-stabilizing processes. Finally, we give the analysis sketch in Section 5. All the algorithms and their full analysis are provided in the Appendix.

1.1 Our Contributions

We take the first steps towards efficiently and robustly augmenting advice for efficient recovery of P2P networks. Specifically, we provide self-stabilizing algorithms for graph linearization, which has been a foundation (i.e., an intermediate step) for many self-stabilizing networks (see, a recent survey of [30]). Our solution achieves an optimal self-stabilization time if the supervisor is honest; otherwise, it retains the self-stabilization time of any solution without supervision.

To that end, we develop a novel and generic approach in which the supervisor needs to send only one O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-bit sized advice message to any peer, where nn denotes the network size. Surprisingly, despite this small advice, peers can quickly build a hypercubic structure that can be used to securely create new connections among peers. Specifically, every peer connects to its neighbor(s) in the sorted line network in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, if the advice messages are correct; otherwise, each peer rejects its advice in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, and stops making any additional edge manipulations due to that advice. This is done in part by an interesting connection to the field of proof-labeling schemes [52], and the following key technical ingredient (which may be of independent interest) for overlay networks.

Theorem 1.1 (Informal, Tree-to-Path).

There is a distributed algorithm for forming a path overlay from a (labelled) tree overlay in O⁡(1)O(1) rounds, whilst adding O⁡(1)O(1) edges per peer.

For robustness against a (potentially) malicious supervisor, the peers (simultaneously) run a “base algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0},” which when run independently (i.e., without any supervisor) is known to self-stabilize in R⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) rounds. When a peer receives an advice message, it executes a set of algorithms (cf. Section 4), designed to expedite the base algorithm, so that the network can quickly self-stabilize. Combined with our design of advice, we get the following upper bounds (based on the supervisor) for converging to the sorted line network.

Theorem 1.2 (Upper Bound).

The network self-stabilizes in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds if the supervisor is honest; otherwise, the network self-stabilizes in O⁡(R⁡(𝒜0)+log⁡n)O(\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0})+\log n) rounds.

Finally, we prove that this logarithmic convergence time barrier is unavoidable for any algorithm if the advice can be arbitrarily corrupted. In particular, since a malicious supervisor could potentially inject adversarial ids into the system [25], a peer must not make connections to any arbitrary peer id given in the advice. Thus, this constraint, that new edges can only be added to any peer’s current neighborhood, leads to the following lower bound (for converging to any network).

Theorem 1.3 (Lower Bound).

There exists some initial configuration such that the convergence time for any pair of supervisor and overlay algorithms is Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) rounds.

1.2 Related Work

Peer-to-peer (P2P) systems have been in the spotlight for several decades (see, e.g., [71, 74, 70, 59, 62]), due to their multifaceted architectures that give rise to different algorithmic challenges in many distributed systems, including but not limited to load-balancing (e.g., [48, 28]), overlay networks (e.g., [68, 61]), agreement (e.g., [6, 7]), publish/subscribe systems (e.g., [18, 19, 12]), Sybil defense (e.g., [40, 20]), etc.

In many P2P systems, a cornerstone problem is building and maintaining a desirable overlay network. Since these systems need to be highly resilient to failures, researchers have extensively worked on self-stabilizing algorithms for several networks; for e.g., variants of Skip and Chord graphs [49, 44, 9], hypertrees and radix trees [23, 5], small-world graph [50], metric graph [39], etc; for a comprehensive survey, see [30].

Graph linearization is the main building block for many of the above self-stabilizing networks. Specifically, a linearization algorithm (e.g. [67]) forms an ordering of peers (e.g. based on their ids), whose structure is then exploited to build other components of the desired network. To the best of our knowledge, the state-of-the-art algorithm [44] that can recover the sorted line network runs in O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) rounds. Notably, the Transitive Closure Framework (TCF) [10] is a generic approach for the peers to recover any (locally-checkable) network in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, but it is not scalable as it requires the peers to first form a clique network (i.e., each peer’s degree necessarily increases to Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n)), and then converge to the desired network.

Recently, the algorithmic framework of using predictions [65] has gained immense popularity in several fields of algorithms (e.g., [55, 63, 11, 47, 56, 58]) including distributed and networked algorithms, for e.g., contention resolution [38], TCP acknowledgment [41], buffer management [1] and graph algorithms [14]. These algorithms are given an extra string of bits called “prediction” to solve the problem. Typically, the prediction would give information about some “structure” of the given input. However, the main challenge is to design robust algorithms (incl. the prediction) that can retain their original performance regardless of what the prediction is, whilst performing much better if the prediction is helpful.

1.3 Network Model & Problem Definition

Entities.   The system has two entities: nodes and a supervisor.

Nodes are computing entities that aim to distributively form a target topology, denoted by G∗G^{*}, through their connections, where we say that two nodes are “connected” if they can communicate (i.e., send/receive messages) with each other. We colloquially use the word “network” (formally defined soon) to capture the set of nodes and their connections. The number of nodes is denoted by nn. Furthermore, the nodes do not have any global knowledge (e.g., network size, shared clock, etc). The nodes always execute the algorithms prescribed to them.

A supervisor is a single computing entity, designed to help the nodes form the target topology G∗G^{*} through communication with the nodes to learn the (current) network, compute over it, and propose connections between nodes. If the supervisor follows its algorithm, we say that the supervisor is honest; otherwise, it is said to be malicious. There is no restriction on the messages sent by a malicious supervisor, which may even include suggestions for connecting to non-existing nodes.

Node ids.   Each node has a unique identifier (id). Each node’s memory consists of two types of variables: address and non-address variables. The address variables are exclusively used to store the ids of other nodes (referred to as neighbors), whereas the non-address variables cannot be used to store node ids.

Communication Rounds.   The system proceeds in synchronous rounds, i.e., a message sent by a node in any round is received by its recipient at the beginning of the next round. In every round, each node runs the given algorithms, given its variables’ assignments (and messages in the channel), resulting in changes to its memory and new messages being sent.

Comm. among Nodes.   Each node uu can send a message to another node vv if the node uu has node vv’s id in its memory. If a message is sent to any node uu, then it is added to node uu’s channel u.𝐶ℎu.\mathit{Ch}. Once a message is added to any node’s channel, the node is able to read the contents of the message, after which the message is removed from the channel. In general, a node is not informed about the (id of the) sender of a message, unless the sender explicitly adds its own id to the message.

States and Configurations.   Consider the standard state model for self-stabilization [21]. The variables and channel of a node are stored in its register (aka, mutable memory) and each node has read/write access to its register. Each node also has a non-mutable memory that contains its id and the code of our algorithms. The set of values assigned to the variables and channel of a node is called the state of a node. Moreover, the tuple of states of all nodes is called the configuration, and the (simultaneous) execution of the code by all the nodes, over consecutive rounds, forms a sequence of configurations.

As we consider a distributed message-passing system where the communication links can themselves change over time, each node needs to explicitly communicate some information about its own state to (some of) node ids stored in its register, for the network to reach the target topology (see, [44, 30]), unlike in the standard model [21], where every node reads its own register and the registers of all its neighbors, executes the algorithms and updates its register, in any given step.

Communication Graph and Network.   Let GC=(V,ℰC=EC∪IC)G_{C}=(V,\mathcal{E}_{C}=E_{C}\cup I_{C}) be the communication graph over the set of nodes VV in configuration CC, where there exists an explicit edge (u,v)∈EC(u,v)\in E_{C} if a node vv’s id is stored in any address variable of node uu’s memory, or an implicit edge (u,v)∈IC(u,v)\in I_{C} if a node vv’s id is in node uu’s channel. The network is simply the communication graph restricted to explicit edges.

Comm. between Supervisor and Nodes.   The supervisor is aware of the node membership in the system, i.e., ids of all the nodes. It can send a request to any node to learn the (current) communication graph. Moreover, the supervisor can send advice messages to help nodes quickly converge to the desired target topology. As is typical, we assume that the supervisor cannot forge messages sent by nodes.

Functions, Rules and Actions.   Each node runs a sequence of algorithms, and each algorithm consists of a sequence of functions. A function has the form, ⟨Label⟩: ⟨Guard⟩→⟨Rule 1;Rule 2;…⟩\langle\text{Label}\rangle\text{: }\langle\text{Guard}\rangle\rightarrow\langle\text{Rule 1};\text{Rule 2};\dots\rangle, where label is the function name, guard is a Boolean predicate over the node’s variables, and rules define the actions by the node, where an action (typically) refers to either updating a local variable or sending a new message. Each rule is itself of the form ⟨Guard⟩→⟨Action 1;Action 2;…⟩\langle\text{Guard}\rangle\rightarrow\langle\text{Action 1};\text{Action 2};\dots\rangle.

Pseudocodes. Each line in a function is typically dedicated to a single rule, but if there are multiple rules in a line, then the last set of actions in that line belongs to the last rule. Moreover, a function may call another function in any of its rules. (In the standard state model [21], the algorithms are directly defined by a set of rules; we extend it for better readability.)

Local Computation. In each round, each node checks the guard of every function in the specified order; if the guard is satisfied, the node executes the rules in the function. Similarly, a node checks the guard of a rule; if it is satisfied, the node proceeds to execute the actions in it. Whereas, if no guard is specified, the function or rule is always executed.

Problem Definition

Given any (weakly) connected communication graph, the nodes must form (and stay in) the target topology. For graph linearization, the target topology is the network where each node is connected to its neighbor(s) in the sorted order, based on their ids. As the nodes also need to process the advice given by the supervisor, we allow them to store a small number of extra edges, which help in quickly linearizing the network.

Initial, Target and Legal Configurations.   Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} and 𝒯⊆𝒞\mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{C} be the set of all possible configurations and the set of target configurations, respectively. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the set of initial configurations where ∀C∈𝒞,GC​ is weakly connected⇔C∈ℐ\forall C\in\mathcal{C},G_{C}\text{ is weakly connected}\iff C\in\mathcal{I}. (We need only weak connectivity for the initial configuration, so the non-address variables can be arbitrarily corrupted.)

The “sorted path” network [67] is the target topology, G∗=(V,E∗)G^{*}=(V,E^{*}), where ∀u,v∈V,(u=𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐⁡(v)∨v=𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐⁡(u))⇔(u,v)∈E∗\forall u,v\in V,(u=\mathit{succ}(v)\lor v=\mathit{succ}(u))\iff(u,v)\in E^{*}, where 𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐(u)=min({v∣v.𝑖𝑑>u.𝑖𝑑})\mathit{succ}(u)=\min\left(\{v\mid v.\mathit{id}>u.\mathit{id}\}\right). Thus, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the set of configurations where the network is G∗G^{*}.

Let NC​(u)={v∣(u,v)∈EC}N_{C}(u)=\{v\mid(u,v)\in E_{C}\} denote the set of all edges stored by a node uu in any configuration CC. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the set of legal configurations such that for each node uu, ∀C′∈ℒ,∃C∈𝒯,NC​(u)⊆NC′​(u)\forall C^{\prime}\in\mathcal{L},\exists C\in\mathcal{T},N_{C}(u)\subseteq N_{C^{\prime}}(u) and ∀C′∈ℒ,∀C∈𝒯,|NC′​(u)|=O⁡(|NC​(u)|+log⁡n)\forall C^{\prime}\in\mathcal{L},\forall C\in\mathcal{T},|N_{C^{\prime}}(u)|=O(|N_{C}(u)|+\log n). In other words, we allow every node to store at most logarithmic number of extra edges (i.e., besides the edges in the sorted path) in a legal configuration.

Self-Stabilization.   We say that an algorithm is self-stabilizing if the network, starting from any initial configuration, reaches a legal configuration (convergence), and stays in one (closure).

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Dual-State Approach

We rely on a dual-state algorithm design, where the nodes always run a “base algorithm” 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} (in the background), and an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is executed for processing the advice given by the supervisor. Moreover, the base algorithm is known to self-stabilize in R⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) rounds, without any interaction with the supervisor. The objective of algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is to use the advice for introducing the neighbors in G∗G^{*} to each other in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, whilst adding as few additional edges as possible.

We distinguish the memory (including channel) used for the algorithms 𝒜\mathcal{A} and 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} as M⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{M}(\mathcal{A}) and M⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}(\mathcal{A}_{0}), respectively. Since these algorithms are run in tandem, to ensure connectivity for the base algorithm, we define a “Flush” operation, denoted by 𝐅𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐡⁡(⋅)\mathbf{Flush}(\cdot), that moves a given set of node ids to any (arbitrary) address variable(s) of M⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}(\mathcal{A}_{0}); this definition is as general as possible so that our approach works for any base algorithm.

2.2 Universal Overlay Primitives

Let us recall the four universal communication primitives (for edge manipulations) in the design of distributed self-stabilizing overlay algorithms (see, e.g., [72, 30]); see Figure 2.

While preserving connectivity, they are used to transform any weakly connected graph to any other weakly connected graph.

2.3 Local Certification of Spanning Tree

Our algorithm for the supervised setting exploits a classic result in distributed computing: local certification of spanning tree [3]. In general, in local certification, there exist a prover and a distributed verifier (fixed network of nodes). The prover assigns a small certificate to each node. Every node inspects its certificate and the certificates of its neighbors to verify a given network property (e.g., spanning tree). If that property is specified correctly at each node, there exists a certificate assignment so that each node “accepts” its certificate; otherwise, regardless of what certificates are assigned by the prover, at least one node “rejects” its certificate. If the verification algorithm has access to the node id, that type of certification is called proof-labeling scheme [52]. For more details, we refer to a recent survey [31].

Specifically, for each node, a certificate for a spanning tree, with any node chosen as the root, consists of the information: id of the root, id of the parent (in that tree), and distance of the node from the root. To locally verify the encoded spanning tree, each node carries out two checks: (1) every neighboring node has the same root id, and (2) its distance is one more than the distance of its parent (called “distance-check”); and the root node checks that its distance is 0.

3 Sybil Resistant, Compact and Robust Advice

Here, we provide the key intuition and details of the advice.

3.1 Network Snapshot and Properties of Advice

First, if the supervisor does not know anything about the current communication graph, there is no hope of giving useful advice because the supervisor should be restricted to a node’s neighborhood whenever an edge is proposed. However, as P2P systems are dynamic, the communication graph could have changed. Thus, there should be some mechanism where the nodes can send their neighborhoods when requested by the supervisor. Once the neighborhood is sent, a node can maintain it for O⁡(1)O(1) rounds, while continuing to run the base algorithm. (The details on this interaction with the supervisor are given in Section A.2.2.) For simplicity, we assume that the supervisor has access to a snapshot of the network, on which the advice can be computed, and that the snapshot is maintained by the nodes.

Given any network snapshot, the supervisor can compute a (close to) minimum sequence of the universal primitives (cf. Section 2.2), so that the network forms the target topology (see [72] for details). However, since the nodes do not have any global information (e.g., round number, etc), they would need to fully trust the supervisor for proposing appropriate edges to eventually form the target topology. This can be problematic for the convergence time as well as the number of edges stored by the nodes over time. Thus, there should be some mechanism by which a node can quickly verify whether the proposed edges are indeed helpful, whilst also limiting the number of additional edges stored due to the supervisor.

Desirable Properties.   Based on these insights, we propose that the advice message at any given node has the following properties to achieve both efficiency and robustness.

  1. 1.

    Sybil-Resistant. For each node uu, and for any node id vv present in node uu’s advice message but not present in node uu’s memory or channel, node uu neither assigns vv to any variable (i.e. store in its memory), nor sends vv to any other node (i.e., circulate it in the network).

  2. 2.

    Compact. Size of the advice is small, i.e., a message of size at most O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) bits is given to each node.

  3. 3.

    Robust. If any node received an incorrect advice, every node rejects its advice (if that node had received advice), and restores the dedicated memory for handling advice (i.e., memory M⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{M}(\mathcal{A})), in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds; whereas, if every node received correct advice, the nodes will be in a legal configuration in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

3.2 Building a Global Structure from any Snapshot

Given the properties of advice, we describe two immediate challenges towards designing the advice. First, we should be able to connect every pair of nodes that are adjacent in the sorted-path topology but may be situated far away from each other in any given snapshot, in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. Second, if any node received an incorrect advice, the other nodes should be informed about it in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds by a scalable mechanism so that they can also quickly reject their advice.

One can observe that the above challenges arise from a lack of a global structure in the network. Thus, our first attempt is to build a lightweight structure, specifically a hypercube, from the advice given to the nodes. Building a hypercubic overlay can be used to “kill two birds with one stone”: first, a node can rely on a local routing algorithm, where a message from a source is forwarded to the next node and so on until it reaches the destination, to initiate a new connection (e.g., for forming the sorted path); second, if a node detects any fault with the advice, it can quickly inform the other nodes in the hypercube, after which the nodes can leave the hypercubic structure.

Now, we enlist the steps for building a hypercubic structure.

  1. 1.

    Snapshot to Tree. Supervisor chooses a rooted spanning tree in the snapshot. As part of the advice, each node is given the id of its parent and the distance to the root.

  2. 2.

    Tree to Path. Each node performs a local transformation (see Section 3.4, for the Tree-to-Path algorithm), so that all the nodes are part of a single path. As part of the advice, nodes are given unique “virtual ids,” going from 1 to nn, from one end of that path to the other.

  3. 3.

    Path to Hypercube. By a pointer-doubling approach [46] (over that path), each node hierarchically introduces its neighbors to each other. Thus, in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, every node connects to “shortcuts,” at distances of 1,2,4,…1,2,4,\dots from it, forming what we call a ‘‘flyover’’ which is a hypercubic structure11 1 Note that a hypercube is technically defined for a network size that is a power of 2. In general, flyover belongs to a family of hypercubic networks, and that path and collection of shortcut edges contain the hypercube edges.; for e.g., see Figure 3.

  4. 4.

    Routing. Once the nodes form a flyover, every node can route messages to any other node [57] (c.f. Figure 3), using the virtual ids and shortcuts, in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

At this point, an astute reader may note that multiple flyovers could form in different parts of the network, whereas some nodes may not even have received any advice. Such concurrency issues are exactly what makes this problem of handling a malicious supervisor difficult. In Section 4.2, we outline how this flyover is carefully constructed and verified, and how small information (i.e., a unique identifier for flyover) is exchanged between the nodes (within and outside the flyover), to quickly detect faulty advice.

3.3 Locally Verifying the Advised sorted Path

After we have a desriable global structure (i.e., all the nodes forming a flyover over a sequentially numbered path), one natural approach is that for each node, as part of its advice, send the virtual id (i.e., position on that numbered path) of its neighbor(s) in the target topology. Each node can then quickly route its own id over the hypercubic structure to the node with that virtual id to create a new connection, thereby forming the “advised” target topology. But as the nodes have a local view, they cannot easily verify if the actual target topology was indeed formed.

For example, let the sorted path be (u1,u2,…,un)(u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{n}), where u1u_{1} is the node with the smallest node id. If the advice for node uiu_{i} consists of the virtual ids of nodes ui−1u_{i-1} and ui+1u_{i+1}, the node uiu_{i} can send its own node id to them via “hypercubic routing” (by virtual ids and shortcuts; e.g., see Figure 3) [57], and make a connection to them. Once these edges are added, each node can locally verify that it has at most 2 edges, and if it has 2 edges, it is the “middle” node id (in sorted order). But a bad supervisor can give advice so that the paths (u1,…,un/2)(u_{1},\dots,u_{n/2}) and (un/2,…,un)(u_{n/2},\dots,u_{n}) are formed, without any node detecting any fault with the advice. In other words, the “advised” sorted path (i.e., connections suggested by the supervisor via virtual ids) do not form a single connected component. Being able to (distributively) detect if any two components of the overlay are connected, is a non-trivial task with the best-known technique (i.e., linear-probing), requiring O⁡(n)O(n) rounds [30].

To fix such connectivity-related issues in the advised sorted path, we make use of local certification of a spanning tree (cf. Section 2.3). Specifically, the sorted path G∗G^{*} is encoded as a rooted spanning tree called “sorted-path tree T∗T^{*},” where the root is the node whose virtual id is 1. As part of advice, each node is given the virtual id of its parent, and the distance to the root, in the tree T∗T^{*}. See Algorithm 1, and Figure 4 for a pictorial example. In local certification, the verification of the certificates is carried out over a fixed network, but in our case, the nodes in T∗T^{*} may not even be connected. Thus, each node uses the hypercubic structure for routing and connecting to its parent in T∗T^{*}. Moreover, that structure is also used to quickly disseminate the node id of the root in T∗T^{*} to all the nodes. In Section 4.3, we explain how the formation and verification of the tree T∗T^{*} is accomplished via routing over the hypercubic structure.

3.4 Tree-to-Path Algorithm

Let T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) be a labelled rooted undirected tree, where VV is the set of vertices, r∈Vr\in V is the root, l(⋅): V→{0,1}l(\cdot)\text{: }V\rightarrow\{0,1\} is a label function on vertices where l⁡(v)=(l⁡(r)+dist⁡(r,v))mod2l(v)=(l(r)+\mathrm{dist}(r,v))\mod 2, and EE is the set of edges. Let CT​(v)={u∣dist⁡(u,v)=1∧dist⁡(v,r)<dist⁡(u,r)}C_{T}(v)=\{u\mid\mathrm{dist}(u,v)=1\wedge\mathrm{dist}(v,r)<\mathrm{dist}(u,r)\} be the children of v∈Vv\in V in the tree TT, and there is a total order (for e.g., based on ids) on CT​(v)={u1,…,uq}C_{T}(v)=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{q}\} such that u1<⋯<uqu_{1}<\dots<u_{q} for any q≥1q\geq 1. Let Beg⁡(P)\mathrm{Beg}(P) and End⁡(P)\mathrm{End}(P) of a directed path PP of size at least 2, denote the vertex with no incoming edge and the vertex with no outgoing edge, respectively.

We briefly describe the Tree-to-Path algorithm that takes a labelled rooted tree as input, and outputs a directed path. See Figure 5 for the pictorial description. Specifically, the algorithm takes in a tree T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) as input, and outputs a directed path PP where Beg⁡(P)=r\mathrm{Beg}(P)=r and End⁡(P)=min⁡(CT​(r))\mathrm{End}(P)=\min(C_{T}(r)) if l⁡(r)=0l(r)=0, whereas it outputs a directed path PP where Beg⁡(P)=max⁡(CT​(r))\mathrm{Beg}(P)=\max(C_{T}(r)) and End⁡(P)=r\mathrm{End}(P)=r if l⁡(r)=1l(r)=1. We incorporate this alternation based on labels for maintaining the invariant that Beg⁡(P)\mathrm{Beg}(P) and End⁡(P)\mathrm{End}(P) are at a distance of 1. Such a simple, fast and local algorithm is amenable to be made self-stabilizing. In Section A.2.2, we give the self-stabilizing version of the algorithm that converts any (connected) overlay to a path overlay, using the given advice, in O⁡(1)O(1) rounds.

4 Flyovers: Fast Stabilization via Routing

We rely on the dual-state approach (cf. Section 2.1), where a node executes a set of algorithms (for handling the advice) for helping the base algorithm to quickly form the sorted path.

In this section, we give the intuition and pseudocodes for three self-stabilizing processes, that are concurrently executed to help the nodes form the sorted path in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, if the advice is correct; otherwise, every node ignores the advice in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, whilst still executing the base algorithm. Before delving into the details, we outline the design of our solution, and also describe the roles of all the variables for it.

4.1 Variables, High-Level Design, and Initialization

We refer to the hypercubic structure that a node belongs to as a flyover, as the nodes “bypass” the current network to find “short paths” to other nodes. Recall that a flyover is built on some path (over all the nodes) formed due to the advice (cf. Section 3.4).

Variables.   First, we explain all the variables of any node uu that make up a flyover.

  1. 1.

    u.Lu.L and u.Ru.R denote the sets of left and right shortcuts (resp.); recall, shortcuts are node ids that are at distance 1,2,4,…1,2,4,\dots on the path. u.S=u.L∪u.Ru.S=u.L\cup u.R is the set of all shortcuts. Moreover, we refer to u.Sl​(i)u.S_{l}(i) and u.Sr​(i)u.S_{r}(i) as the “ii-level” left and right shortcut (resp.).

  2. 2.

    u.𝑣𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{vID} is used for storing the virtual id; recall, the virtual id is provided in the advice, which is used to determine its position on the path. (This is not to be confused with the unique id of a node, see Section 1.3; when we just refer to “id,” we mean the unique id of the node.) By design, the node with no left shortcut has virtual id 1.

  3. 3.

    u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} is used for storing a “unique identifier” for the flyover, called the flyover id. By design, the node id of the node with no left shortcut, determines the flyover id.

  4. 4.

    u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡u.\mathit{exit} is a binary variable indicating if the node should exit the flyover. If any node exits the flyover, it runs only the base algorithm (until it receives a new advice).

We also use three variables for storing and verifying what we refer to as connectivity certificate, based on the local certification of spanning tree; these variables are used for certifying the sorted-path tree T∗T^{*}. (Algorithm 1 has the definition of T∗T^{*}.)

  1. 1.

    u.c-paru.\textit{c-par} is used for storing the virtual id of the parent of node uu in the sorted-path tree T∗T^{*}.

  2. 2.

    u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} is used for storing the distance from the root to node uu in the sorted-path tree T∗T^{*}.

  3. 3.

    u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids} is used for storing the node ids of node uu’s neighbors in the sorted-path topology G∗G^{*}.

Our Design.   A node uu updates the variables u.vID,u.c-paru.\textit{vID},u.\textit{c-par} and u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} (if it’s not part of a flyover) when it receives the advice. (See Algorithm 1 for how those values are determined.) The Tree-to-Path algorithm is then executed, and based on its position, the first left and right shortcuts, i.e., u.Sl​(1)u.S_{l}(1) and u.Sr​(1)u.S_{r}(1), are updated to its left and right neighbors on the path (resp.). Subsequently, the nodes build the flyover over the path via pointer-doubling, where the (i+1)(i+1)-level shortcuts are formed from the ii-level shortcuts; see Figure 3. By design, the node id of the “leftmost” node (in the path), say, node vv with v.L=∅∧v.R≠∅v.L=\emptyset\land v.R\neq\emptyset, is the flyover id, and is propagated to the rest of the nodes in flyover, i.e., for any node uu, u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} is initially assigned its own node id (as a default value), but is eventually assigned the flyover id. Moreover, node vv is the only node with v.𝑣𝐼𝐷=1v.\mathit{vID}=1 and v.c-dist=0v.\textit{c-dist}=0, as it is the root in the sorted-path tree T∗T^{*}. See Figure 4 for an illustration.

To verify the connectivity certificate, i.e., execute distance-checks (cf. Section 3.3), each node u≠vu\neq v must send the distance u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} to the node with virtual id u.c-paru.\textit{c-par}, say node ww, on the flyover. However, since node uu may not have a direct connection to node ww, it sends u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} to the closest left or right shortcut (depending on the virtual ids, i.e., u.vIDu.\textit{vID} and u.c-paru.\textit{c-par}), and so on, until this message eventually reaches node ww whose virtual id is u.c-paru.\textit{c-par}. This is a standard method for routing a message between any pair of nodes in a hypercubic structure [57], on which we further provide details below. Finally, once the node ww receives this message, it adds node id uu to w.c-idsw.\textit{c-ids} if the distances match, i.e., w.c-dist=u.c-dist−1w.\textit{c-dist}=u.\textit{c-dist}-1 (to form the sorted path). Moreover, every node uu checks that it is sorted with respect to node ids in u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids} (to verify the sorted path).

Init Function.   Our design results in a few simple tests that are executed in every round; see Algorithm 2. Here, the 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩⁡(x)\mathbf{NextStop}(x) function returns the ii-level left or right shortcut, whose virtual id, u.𝑣𝐼𝐷±2iu.\mathit{vID}\pm 2^{i}, is closest to xx; if it is not possible to do so (e.g., u.𝑣𝐼𝐷<xu.\mathit{vID}<x and a right shortcut does not exist), then the function returns “∅\varnothing”. see Algorithm 3 for its description. Observe that if any of the tests fail, u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡u.\mathit{exit} is updated to 1. In that case, node uu rejects the flyover, i.e., it sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle message to all the node ids, flushes those ids (see Section 2.1 for the “flush” operation), and sets all the variables to the default values.

4.2 Construction and Verification of Flyover

Here, we explain the first two self-stabilizing processes concerned with the flyover structure. As the flyover is symmetrically built over some path, for readability, we provide the explanations with respect to right shortcuts (if they exist), which similarly apply for left shortcuts. Recall that if a node vv is a ii-level (right) shortcut of node uu, then node vv should be of distance 2i2^{i} to (the right of) node uu on the path.

Our algorithms consist of a precise set of conditions for both, sending a particular message, and for specific actions to be taken (for e.g., update the set of shortcuts, or set the exit variable to 1) after receiving a message. Moreover, if any node uu is not part of any flyover (i.e., u.S=∅u.S=\emptyset), and receives a message regarding a flyover, then node uu sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle message to the node ids part of that message, and flushes them.

Algorithm 4 provides the sequence of rules that govern the construction of the flyover.

A node uu sends its own node id to its first right shortcut, u.Sr​(1)u.S_{r}(1), using the ⟨TestLine-R⟩\langle\text{TestLine-R}\rangle message, to verify whether that information is correct. Consequently, the node that receives the message, sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle message to node uu, and flushes it, if node uu is not its left neighbor.

A node uu sends its ii-level left shortcut u.Sl​(i)u.S_{l}(i), including its own id, to its ii-level right shortcut u.Sr​(i)u.S_{r}(i), using ⟨FlyConst-R⟩\langle\text{FlyConst-R}\rangle message, so that u.Sr​(i)u.S_{r}(i) can add or verify its (i+1)(i+1)-level left shortcut. This set of rules facilitates a pointer-doubling style, bottom-up flyover construction over the path (regardless of any shortcuts that may already exist). Consequently, the node that receives the message, say node ww, sets w.Sl​(i+1)=u.Sl​(i)w.S_{l}(i+1)=u.S_{l}(i) only if |w.L|=i|w.L|=i and w.Sl​(i)=uw.S_{l}(i)=u; otherwise, it sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to nodes uu and u.Sl​(i)u.S_{l}(i), and flushes them.

Algorithm 5 gives the sequence of rules for the verification of virtual id and flyover id.

A node uu sends the value 2(i−1)+u.𝑣𝐼𝐷2^{(i-1)}+u.\mathit{vID} to node u.Sr​(i)u.S_{r}(i), using ⟨TestvID⟩\langle\text{TestvID}\rangle message, to verify the distance of its ii-level right shortcut (over the path that the flyover is constructed on). Consequently, the node that receives the message, say node ww, sets w.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1w.\mathit{exit}=1 if its virtual id does not match the value.

A node uu sends its u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} (flyover id), using ⟨TestFlyID⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID}\rangle message, to all node ids, except u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID}, in memory (incl. Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}), memory of base algorithm), if either node uu is the leftmost node, or u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} has been updated (i.e., u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷≠u.𝑖𝑑u.\mathit{flyID}\neq u.\mathit{id}). Furthermore, a node uu, when it is ready to receive advice from the supervisor (i.e., u.S=∅∧u.𝑣𝐼𝐷=0u.S=\emptyset\land u.\mathit{vID}=0), sends “⊥\bot” to all the node ids using ⟨TestFlyID⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID}\rangle message. Crucially, this exchange of information (i.e., flyover id) acts as a simple mechanism for handling a supervisor that concurrently sends bad advice to nodes in different parts of the network, in that it helps the nodes quickly detect if there is a flyover constructed over any subset of nodes. Consequently, the node that receives the message, say node ww, sets w.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷w.\mathit{flyID} to u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID}, only if it is not the leftmost node, and w.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷w.\mathit{flyID} has not been updated yet (i.e., w.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷w.\mathit{flyID} is assigned to w.𝑖𝑑w.\mathit{id}). Finally, if w.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷w.\mathit{flyID} does not match u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID}, node ww sets w.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1w.\mathit{exit}=1, and sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle message to node u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID}, and flushes it.

4.3 Verification of Connectivity Certificate

Here, we explain the self-stabilizing process for verifying and forming the sorted-path topology.

Algorithm 6 provides the sequence of rules for routing and verifying connectivity certificates.

First, each node uu begins this process after its flyover id u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} has been updated (i.e., u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷≠u.𝑖𝑑u.\mathit{flyID}\neq u.\mathit{id}). Recall that each node uu sends u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID}, via ⟨TestFlyID⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID}\rangle message, to all node ids in memory, to ensure that a single flyover exists. Thus, the node id of the root in tree T∗T^{*} (i.e., node with virtual id 1; see Algorithm 1) gets stored and verified by each node.

A node uu needs to send u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} (i.e., distance to the root in T∗T^{*}), to the node with virtual id u.c-paru.\textit{c-par}, say node vv. For doing so, the node uu routes both u.c-distu.\textit{c-dist} and u.𝑖𝑑u.\mathit{id}, using ⟨TestCert⟩\langle\text{TestCert}\rangle message, via an appropriate left or right shortcut (based on the virtual ids), and so on, until the message reaches node vv. Recall, 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩⁡(x)\mathbf{NextStop}(x) returns the ii-level left or right shortcut, whose virtual id, u.𝑣𝐼𝐷±2iu.\mathit{vID}\pm 2^{i}, is closest to xx. In a hypercubic structure, a message can be routed this way in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, as the distance to the intended destination is halved each time.

Consequently, the node that receives the message, say node w≠vw\neq v, assigns w.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1w.\mathit{exit}=1, and sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle message to node uu, if the message cannot be further forwarded (i.e., 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩(u.c-par)\mathbf{NextStop}(u.\textit{c-par}) function returns “∅\varnothing”). Finally, when the node vv receives it, if the virtual ids and distances match (i.e., v.𝑣𝐼𝐷=u.c-parv.\mathit{vID}=u.\textit{c-par} and v.c-dist=u.c-dist−1v.\textit{c-dist}=u.\textit{c-dist}-1), node vv adds the node id uu to v.c-idsv.\textit{c-ids}, and sends its own node id to node uu, so that node uu stores it in u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids}; otherwise, the node vv sets v.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1v.\mathit{exit}=1, and sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to node uu, and flushes it.

5 Analysis Sketch

In this section, we describe the analysis sketch for all the critical aspects of our algorithms. The pseudocodes are given in Section A, and the full analyses are given in Section B and C.

Firstly, we show that the edges added by the Tree-to-Path algorithm (c.f. Figure 5; see Algorithm 10 for the pseudocode.) form a single (directed) path over the nodes. We use a proof by induction over the height of a labbelled rooted tree. We consider two base cases for the trees of height equal to 1, with the label of the root equal to either 0 or 1, where the height of a tree T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) is equal to maxv∈V⁡(distT​(r,v))\max_{v\in V}(\mathrm{dist}_{T}(r,v)). For the inductive case, we consider any tree T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) of height greater than 1, and then show that the algorithm outputs a directed path PP where Beg⁡(P)=r\mathrm{Beg}(P)=r and End⁡(P)\mathrm{End}(P) is min⁡(CT​(r))\min(C_{T}(r)) if l⁡(r)=0l(r)=0; whereas it outputs a directed path PP where Beg⁡(P)\mathrm{Beg}(P) is max⁡(CT​(r))\max(C_{T}(r)) and End⁡(P)=r\mathrm{End}(P)=r if l⁡(r)=1l(r)=1.

Theorem 5.1.

The Tree-to-Path Algorithm takes a labelled rooted tree T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) where l⁡(r)=0l(r)=0 as input, and outputs a directed path P=(V,E′)P=(V,E^{\prime}) where Beg⁡(P)=r\mathrm{Beg}(P)=r and End⁡(P)=min⁡(CT​(r))\mathrm{End}(P)=\min(C_{T}(r)).

Next, we show that the construction of shortcuts over that path happens in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, implying that information (e.g., ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle messages) can be quickly disseminated in any flyover. Thus, if the flyover is not correctly built, i.e., virtual ids are not consecutive, or shortcuts are not exponentially spaced-out, or flyover id is not properly assigned, then due to Algorithms 2, 4 and 5, some node detects and propagates the fault in the flyover, cueing other nodes to also exit the flyover.

However, if a flyover is “internally correct,” and is formed over a subset of nodes, then some key information needs to be exchanged between the nodes inside and outside the flyover. To that end, we rely on Algorithm 5 where every node sends its flyover id to all node ids in the memory. As all our algorithms rely on the universal primitives (cf. Section 2.2) that preserve (weak) connectivity, there must exist an (incoming/outgoing) edge to that flyover in any round. By carefully carrying out a case-by-case analysis of how that edge can show up in a node’s memory, we prove the following lemma.

Lemma 5.2.

Consider any set of nodes B={v1,…,v|B|}B=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{|B|}\} in any round rr, where |B|<n|B|<n and (v1.L=∅∧v|B|.R=∅)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\land v_{|B|}.R=\emptyset) and (∀i∈[|B|−1],vi.Sr(1)=vi+1∧vi+1.Sl(1)=vi)(\forall i\in[|B|-1],v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}\land v_{i+1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{i}). By round r+O⁡(log⁡n)r+O(\log n), at least one node u∈Bu\in B assigns u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1u.\mathit{exit}=1.

Moreover, we prove that if all the nodes indeed form a single flyover, but if the connections suggested by the supervisor (via virtual ids) do not form G∗G^{*} (see Section 3.3 for a discussion), then due to Algorithms 2 and 6 (i.e., routing the connectivity certificates), at least one node quickly detects the bad advice.

Claim 5.3.

Let V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\} and (v1.L=∅∧vn.R=∅)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\land v_{n}.R=\emptyset) and (∀i∈[n−1],vi.Sr(1)=vi+1∧vi+1.Sl(1)=vi)(\forall i\in[n-1],v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}\land v_{i+1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{i}) and (∀i∈[n],vi.𝑣𝐼𝐷=i∧vi.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=v1)(\forall i\in[n],v_{i}.\mathit{vID}=i\land v_{i}.\mathit{flyID}=v_{1}). Let G′=(V,E′)G^{\prime}=(V,E^{\prime}) such that (u,v)∈E′⇔(u.𝑣𝐼𝐷=v.c-par∧v.c-dist=u.c-dist+1)∨(v.𝑣𝐼𝐷=u.c-par∧v.c-dist=u.c-dist−1)(u,v)\in E^{\prime}\iff(u.\mathit{vID}=v.\textit{c-par}\land v.\textit{c-dist}=u.\textit{c-dist}+1)\lor(v.\mathit{vID}=u.\textit{c-par}\land v.\textit{c-dist}=u.\textit{c-dist}-1). If ∀i∈[n]∖{1},∃ui∈V,vi.c-par=ui.𝑣𝐼𝐷\forall i\in[n]\setminus\{1\},\exists u_{i}\in V,v_{i}.\textit{c-par}=u_{i}.\mathit{vID} where (ui.c-dist=vi.c-dist−1)(u_{i}.\textit{c-dist}=v_{i}.\textit{c-dist}-1), then G′G^{\prime} is same as G∗G^{*}.

Proof Sketch.

Due to Algorithm 2, the following invariants are satisfied for each node u∈Vu\in V.

  1. 1.

    (Tree Distance) (u.L=∅⟹u.c-dist=0)(u.L=\emptyset\implies u.\textit{c-dist}=0) and (u.L≠∅⟹u.c-dist>0)(u.L\neq\emptyset\implies u.\textit{c-dist}>0).

  2. 2.

    (Degree Constraint; Locally Sorted) E′′(u)≠∅⟹(|E′′(u)|=1)∨(|E′′(u)|=2∧min(|E′′(u)|)<u.𝑖𝑑<max(|E′′(u)|))E^{\prime\prime}(u)\neq\emptyset\implies(|E^{\prime\prime}(u)|=1)\lor(|E^{\prime\prime}(u)|=2\land\min(|E^{\prime\prime}(u)|)<u.\mathit{id}<\max(|E^{\prime\prime}(u)|)), where E′′​(u)={v∣(u,v)∈E′}E^{\prime\prime}(u)=\{v\mid(u,v)\in E^{\prime}\}.

The above invariants ensure that there can be only one node uu with u.c-dist=0u.\textit{c-dist}=0, and that node is v1v_{1}. Moreover, the degree of any node in G′G^{\prime} is at most 2; if a node’s degree is 2, then its own id is neither greater nor less than both the node ids of its neighbors. Given the premise of the lemma, for any node u∈V∖{v1}u\in V\setminus\{v_{1}\}, there is a node p⁡(u)p(u) such that u.c-par=p⁡(u).𝑣𝐼𝐷u.\textit{c-par}=p(u).\mathit{vID} and p⁡(u).c-dist=u.c-dist−1p(u).\textit{c-dist}=u.\textit{c-dist}-1.

We use proof by contradiction to show that G′G^{\prime} is indeed G∗G^{*}. First, there cannot be a cycle in G′G^{\prime}, as the distance checks (i.e., from a node uu to its parent p⁡(u)p(u)) cannot be satisfied at all the nodes (cf. Section 2.3). Moreover, G′G^{\prime} cannot be a spanning forest because all the nodes, via flyover id, can verify that there is only one “root node,” which is node v1v_{1} with its distance v1.c-dist=0v_{1}.\textit{c-dist}=0. Thus, G′G^{\prime} forms a spanning tree. Combining the second invariant mentioned earlier, i.e., each node has degree at most 2, the tree must be a path. Finally, that path has to be the sorted path G∗G^{*} due to the second invariant because every node checks that its locally sorted with its neighbors in G′G^{\prime}. ∎

Finally, we give a lower bound on the convergence time given that the nodes are restricted to make edge manipulations in their current neighborhood. The key observation is that if the distance between any two nodes uu and vv is DD in round rr, the distance between them is at least D/2tD/2^{t} in round r+tr+t, even if all nodes introduce all the node ids in their memory to each other in every round. Thus, if the nodes uu and vv should be adjacent in the target topology, it takes Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) rounds for node uu to obtain the node id vv (or vice versa) in the worst-case.

Theorem 5.4.

For any Sybil-resistant network, there exists an initial configuration such that the convergence time for any pair of supervisor and overlay algorithms is Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) rounds.

Appendix A Pseudocodes

In every round, each node executes the flyover algorithms (cf. Section A.1), distributed Tree-to-Path algorithms (cf. Section A.2.2), and then the base algorithm (in that order). In Section D, we outline the list of all variables used by our algorithms.

Transferring the “advised” neighbors to base algorithm.   For any node uu, the variable u.c-idu.\textit{c-id} is used to store its neighbors on the “advised” topology (i.e., connections made by routing over the hypercubic structure due to the advice). Thus, in every round, the ids stored in that variable (if it is nonempty) are added to the address variable(s) of the base algorithm, used to store the neighbors of the target topology, before the algorithm is executed. If the supervisor is honest, this helps the nodes obtain the explicit edges required for the base algorithm to stabilize. However, if the advice is corrupted in any way, then by design, all nodes reject their advice (i.e. execute 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{RejectFlyover} function) in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, and for any node uu, u.c-idu.\textit{c-id} becomes empty.

Choice of base algorithm.   In general, any base algorithm that self-stabilizes to the sorted line using the overlay primitives (cf. Section 2.2) can be chosen. We only require that the algorithm use the Delegate-after-Reversal or DR primitive (cf. Definition C.7), in place of the Delegate primitive, to facilitate information exchange in both directions. (Note that this mechanism is already part of many existing algorithms, including [67, 44].) The DR primitive first delegates an edge in the reverse direction, and then it is immediately set to the intended direction. This primitive can either be implemented in a single round with a “preprocessing” phase (where the edge-reversal happens; see, e.g., Skip+ algorithm [44] where nodes create bidirected links in such a phase), or simply in two rounds in our model.

As examples, if the base algorithm is the classic Linearization algorithm [67], the network self-stabilizes in O⁡(n)O(n) rounds if the supervisor is malicious; if the base algorithm is the Skip+ algorithm [44] (that converges to a topology where the sorted-path is part of it, and the degree of each node is O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)), the network self-stabilizes in O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n) rounds if the supervisor is malicious. Both of those algorithms can be directly used in our setting.

A.1 Flyover Pseudocode

A.2 Tree-to-Path Pseudocode

In this subsection, we first provide the pseudocode of the (centralized) Tree-to-Path algorithm described in Section 3.4. Then, we give the pseudocode for the distributed implementation of the same algorithm, which also includes the interaction with the supervisor.

A.2.1 Sequential Tree-to-Path

A.2.2 Distributed Tree-to-Path

Here, we describe the self-stabilizing algorithms for receiving and processing the advice message. We explicitly address the interaction between the supervisor and the nodes, and also show that it can be combined with the rest of the algorithms.

From the (honest) supervisor’s perceptive, if there is any node that is not part of any flyover, and has its exit variable set to 1, that node would request for advice. Once the supervisor receives the first request, it waits for O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds until all the nodes are not part of any flyover, and have their exit variables set to 1. (Note that by design, if the advice or flyover is not correct, every node executes 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{RejectFlyover} function of Algorithm 2 in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds; see Section C.8 in the analysis.) At this point, the supervisor learns the “network snapshot,” by requesting each node to send its neighborhood, that is, the ids stored in its memory or channel.

From the perspective of any node uu, to avoid being unnecessarily contacted by the supervisor, it should not be part of any flyover (that is, u.S≠∅u.S\neq\emptyset), nor should its u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡u.\mathit{exit} variable be set to 1, while processing an advice message (i.e., during the interaction with the supervisor). After being requested for the neighborhood by the supervisor, every node can store and maintain its current neighborhood for O⁡(1)O(1) rounds to process the advice given by the supervisor. This is achieved by setting and tracking a “timer” variable that indicates that the advice is being processed.

We explain the additional variables of a node uu that are used in the following algorithms.

  1. 1.

    u.tu.t is used as a timer variable which is set to 55 when the supervisor requests for its current neighborhood; u.tu.t is decremented by 1 in every round, until it becomes 0 again.

  2. 2.

    u.𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡u.\mathit{dist} is used for storing the distance from the root, in a rooted spanning tree of the current snapshot, given by the supervisor; see Algorithm 1 for the details. This distance is primarily used by nodes for calculating the label in the Tree-to-Path algorithm (cf. Section 3.4), and is also used for quickly checking that any subset of “parent” ids (in the advice) do not form a cycle, using the distance-checks in local certification (cf. Section 3).

A.3 Helper Functions

Appendix B Tree-to-Path Analysis

Theorem B.1.

Algorithm 10 takes a (labelled) rooted tree T=(l⁡(⋅),r,V,E)T=(l(\cdot),r,V,E) where l⁡(r)=0l(r)=0 as input, and outputs a directed path graph P=(V,E′)P=(V,E^{\prime}), where Beg⁡(P)=r\mathrm{Beg}(P)=r and End⁡(P)=min⁡(CT​(r))\mathrm{End}(P)=\min(C_{T}(r)).

Proof.

The height of a rooted tree TT, denoted by H⁡(T)H(T), is equal to maxv∈V⁡(dist⁡(r,v))\max_{v\in V}(\mathrm{dist}(r,v)). For each node vv, let C⁡(v)={u∣dist⁡(u,v)=1∧dist⁡(v,r)<dist⁡(u,r)}C(v)=\{u\mid\mathrm{dist}(u,v)=1\wedge\mathrm{dist}(v,r)<\mathrm{dist}(u,r)\}. For each node v∈Vv\in V where C⁡(v)≠∅C(v)\neq\emptyset, there is a total ordering (e.g., based on ids) on C⁡(v)={u1,…,uk}C(v)=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\} such that u1<⋯<uku_{1}<\dots<u_{k}.

We inductively prove the following statements over the height of a tree, with the base cases as the set of trees of height 1 (and the label of root can either be 0 or 1).

  1. 1.

    Algorithm 10 takes in any rooted tree Tb=(l⁡(⋅),p,V,E)T_{b}=(l(\cdot),p,V,E) where l⁡(p)=0l(p)=0, and outputs a (directed) path graph P=(V,E′)P=(V,E^{\prime}) where Beg⁡(P)=p\mathrm{Beg}(P)=p and End⁡(P)\mathrm{End}(P) is min⁡(C⁡(p))\min(C(p)) for |V|≥2|V|\geq 2.

Appendix C Self-Stabilization Analysis

C.1 Basic Definitions

Definition C.1.

We use Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) to represent the (internal) memory (including the channel buffer) that a node uu uses for executing algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} respectively. Moreovoer, we use R⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) for the (best-known) upper bound for the (self-stabilization) convergence of the algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} (when it is independently executed).

Definition C.2.

We use the term flyover-related variables to refer to the set of variables in Section A.1. Similarly, we use the term advice-related variables to refer to the set of variables in Section A.2.2.

Definition C.3.

We say that a node uu executes a flush operation on a set of node ids, if it stores them in any set of address variables in Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) (i.e., memory allocated to algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}).

Definition C.4.

Let 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u)\mathit{Adv}(u) be an advice message at node uu. Moreover, when we refer to 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).x=y\mathit{Adv}(u).x=y, then x=yx=y has appeared in the advice. 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u)\mathit{Adv}(u) is said to be well-formed if the following conditions hold.

  1. 1.

    𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑝𝑎𝑟∈{⊥,id}\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{par}\in\{\bot,\mathrm{id}\}, where id\mathrm{id} is present in its memory.

  2. 2.

    If 𝐴𝑑𝑣(u).𝑝𝑎𝑟=⊥\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{par}=\bot, then 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡=0,𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑣𝐼𝐷=1,𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).c-dist=0\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{dist}=0,\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{vID}=1,\mathit{Adv}(u).\textit{c-dist}=0; else 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡>0,𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑣𝐼𝐷>1\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{dist}>0,\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{vID}>1 and 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).c-dist>0\mathit{Adv}(u).\textit{c-dist}>0.

  3. 3.

    𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).𝑣𝐼𝐷∈ℕ\mathit{Adv}(u).\mathit{vID}\in\mathbb{N} and 𝐴𝑑𝑣⁡(u).c-par∈ℕ\mathit{Adv}(u).\textit{c-par}\in\mathbb{N}.

Definition C.5.

We say that a node uu is in dual-state if u.S≠∅u.S\neq\emptyset. Furthermore, if node uu updates a previously non-empty u.Su.S to ∅\emptyset, then we say that node uu has exited from the dual-state.

Definition C.6.

A node uu is said to process an advice message if uu enters Line 6 in Algorithm 12. An advice message, for any node uu, is said to be effective if node uu enters dual-state before u.t≤1u.t\leq 1. We say that a node uu is attentive, or ready to receive advice, if u.S=∅∧u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=0∧u.t=0u.S=\emptyset\land u.\mathit{exit}=0\land u.t=0.

Definition C.7.

(Delegate-after-Reversal; DR Primitive) A node uu is said to use DR primitive for algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} in round rr, if the following conditions hold during the execution of algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}.

  1. 1.

    If node uu is required to delegate an edge (u,w)(u,w) to node vv, i.e., send the id of node ww to node vv, for e.g., via some message ⟨msg,w⟩\langle\mathrm{msg},w\rangle, then (1) node uu first sends ⟨Rev,v,msg,w⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v,\mathrm{msg},w\rangle to node ww, and (2) once node ww receives ⟨Rev,v⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v\rangle, node ww sends its own id to node vv (for e.g., by message ⟨msg,w⟩\langle\mathrm{msg},w\rangle).

  2. 2.

    If node uu is required to send some message ⟨msg,w1,…,w2,…,wt⟩\langle\mathrm{msg},w_{1},\dots,w_{2},\dots,w_{t}\rangle for some t≥1t\geq 1 to node vv, then (1) node uu first sends ⟨Rev,v,msg,w1,…,w2,…,wt⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v,\mathrm{msg},w_{1},\dots,w_{2},\dots,w_{t}\rangle to node w1w_{1}, and for all 1<j≤t1<j\leq t, node uu sends ⟨Rev,v⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v\rangle to node wjw_{j}, and (2) once node w1w_{1} receives ⟨Rev,v,msg,w1,…,w2,…,wt⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v,\mathrm{msg},w_{1},\dots,w_{2},\dots,w_{t}\rangle, node w1w_{1} sends ⟨msg,w1,…,w2,…,wt⟩\langle\mathrm{msg},w_{1},\dots,w_{2},\dots,w_{t}\rangle to node vv, and for all 1<j≤t1<j\leq t, once node wjw_{j} receives ⟨Rev,v⟩\langle\mathrm{Rev},v\rangle, node wjw_{j} sends its own id to node vv.

The message complexity of DR primitive is O⁡(1)O(1) factor to that of “Delegate” primitive (see, e.g., [54]).

Definition C.8.

The network is robust against a supervisor, or s-robust, if these two conditions hold.

  1. 1.

    (Sybil Resistance) For each node uu, and for any node id vv present in node uu’s advice message but not present in node uu’s memory or channel, node uu neither assigns vv to any of its variables (i.e. store in its memory) nor sends vv to any other id present in its memory or channel (i.e., send it to other nodes).

  2. 2.

    (Robustness) If all nodes do not form a single, correctly configured flyover, then all nodes exit the dual-state (thereby rejecting any “supervisor-induced” overlay) in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

C.2 Flyover-Related Definitions

Definition C.9.

We say that a set of nodes B⊆VB\subseteq V is a backbone, where |B|≥2|B|\geq 2, if the following conditions hold. For ease of exposition, wlog, we denote the set BB as {v1,v2,…}\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots\}.

  1. 1.

    (Wings) (v1.L=∅∨v1.Sl(1)∉B)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\lor v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\notin B) and (v|B|.R=∅∨v|B|.Sr(1)∉B)(v_{|B|}.R=\emptyset\lor v_{|B|}.S_{r}(1)\notin B).

  2. 2.

    (Spine) ∀i∈[|B|−1],vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1∧vi+1.Sl​(1)=vi\forall i\in[|B|-1],v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}\land v_{i+1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{i}.

If for all u∈V∖B,u∪Bu\in V\setminus B,u\cup B is not a backbone, then BB is said to be a maximal backbone. A maximal backbone is said to be winged maximal backbone if v1.L≠∅∨v|B|.R≠∅v_{1}.L\neq\emptyset\lor v_{|B|}.R\neq\emptyset.

Definition C.10.

We say that a set of nodes B⊆VB\subseteq V is an ouroboros if any of the following conditions hold. For ease of exposition, wlog, we denote the set BB as {v1,v2,…}\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots\}.

  1. 1.

    (Perfect Ring) (v1.Sl(1)=v|B|∧v|B|.Sr(1)=v1)(v_{1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{|B|}\land v_{|B|}.S_{r}(1)=v_{1}) and ∀i,vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1∧vi+1.Sl​(1)=vi\forall i,v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}\land v_{i+1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{i}.

  2. 2.

    (Stylish Ring) (v1.Sl(1)∈B∨v|B|.Sr(1)∈B)(v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\in B\lor v_{|B|}.S_{r}(1)\in B) and ∀i,vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1∧vi+1.Sl​(1)=vi\forall i,v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}\land v_{i+1}.S_{l}(1)=v_{i}.

If for all u∈V∖B,u∪Bu\in V\setminus B,u\cup B is not an ouroboros, then BB is said to be a maximal ouroboros.

Definition C.11.

An node uu in a dual-state, is said to be lost, if it is not in any backbone or ouroboros.

Definition C.12.

We say that a backbone B⊆VB\subseteq V is a flyover if the following conditions hold. Let v1∈Bv_{1}\in B such that (v1.L=∅∨v1.Sl(1)∈V∖B)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\lor v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\in V\setminus B). For all i∈[|B|−1]i\in[|B|-1], let vi+1∈Bv_{i+1}\in B such that vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}.

  1. 1.

    (Virtual IDs) ∀i∈[|B|−1]\forall i\in[|B|-1], vi+1.𝑣𝐼𝐷=vi.𝑣𝐼𝐷+1v_{i+1}.\mathit{vID}=v_{i}.\mathit{vID}+1.

  2. 2.

    (Hypercube) ∀i∈[|B|−1],∀j∈[⌊log2(|B|−i)⌋+1],(vi.Sr(j)=vi+2j−1∧vi+2j−1.Sl(j)=vi)\forall i\in[|B|-1],\forall j\in\left[\lfloor\log_{2}(|B|-i)\rfloor+1\right],(v_{i}.S_{r}(j)=v_{i+2^{j-1}}\land v_{i+2^{j-1}}.S_{l}(j)=v_{i}).

Definition C.13.

Consider a maximal backbone B={v1,v2,…}⊆VB=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots\}\subseteq V where (v1.L=∅∨v1.Sl(1)∈V∖B)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\lor v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\in V\setminus B) and ∀i∈[|B|−1],vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1\forall i\in[|B|-1],v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}. Let GB∗=(B,EB∗)G^{*}_{B}=(B,E^{*}_{B}) such that (u,v)∈EB∗⇔(u=𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐B​(v)∨v=𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐B​(u))(u,v)\in E^{*}_{B}\iff(u=\mathit{succ}_{B}(v)\lor v=\mathit{succ}_{B}(u)), where 𝑠𝑢𝑐𝑐B(u)=min({w.𝑖𝑑∣(w∈B)∧(w.𝑖𝑑>u.𝑖𝑑)})\mathit{succ}_{B}(u)=\min(\{w.\mathit{id}\mid(w\in B)\land(w.\mathit{id}>u.\mathit{id})\}). Let TB∗T^{*}_{B} be the rooted spanning tree in the graph GB∗G^{*}_{B} with node v1v_{1} as the root. Then, BB is said to be correctly configured if the following conditions hold.

  1. 1.

    ∀i∈[|B|],vi.𝑣𝐼𝐷=i\forall i\in[|B|],v_{i}.\mathit{vID}=i and vi.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=v1.𝑖𝑑v_{i}.\mathit{flyID}=v_{1}.\mathit{id}.

  2. 2.

    ∀i∈[|B|−1],vi.c-par=pi.𝑣𝐼𝐷\forall i\in[|B|-1],v_{i}.\textit{c-par}=p_{i}.\mathit{vID} where pip_{i} denotes the parent of viv_{i} in TB∗T^{*}_{B}.

  3. 3.

    ∀i∈[|B|]\forall i\in[|B|], EB∗​(vi)⊆vi.c-idsE^{*}_{B}(v_{i})\subseteq v_{i}.\textit{c-ids} where E∗​(vi)E^{*}(v_{i}) denotes the edge-set of viv_{i} in GB∗G^{*}_{B}.

  4. 4.

    ∀i∈[|B|],vi.c-dist=𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡TB∗​(vi,v1)\forall i\in[|B|],v_{i}.\textit{c-dist}=\mathit{dist}_{T^{*}_{B}}(v_{i},v_{1}) where 𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡TB∗​(u,v)\mathit{dist}_{T^{*}_{B}}(u,v) is the distance between v1v_{1} and viv_{i} in TB∗T^{*}_{B}.

Definition C.14.

A node uu, with u.S≠∅u.S\neq\emptyset, in round rr, is said to be in a precarious dual-state if any of the following conditions are satisfied.

  1. 1.

    uu is a lost node.

  2. 2.

    uu belongs to a maximal ouroboros.

  3. 3.

    uu belongs to either a maximal backbone of size less than nn, or maximal backbone of size equal to nn but some node sets its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1 in any round r′∈{r,r+1,…​r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉}r^{\prime}\in\{r,r+1,\dots r+3\lceil\log n\rceil\}.

Definition C.15.

The network is said to be stable in any round rr if for each node u∈V,u.S≠∅u\in V,u.S\neq\emptyset but uu is not in a precarious dual-state.

C.3 Helpful Observations

Remark C.16.

For any node uu, the following invariants are ensured (via 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤𝐬\mathbf{BasicChecks} function).

  1. 1.

    u.S=∅⟹u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=u.𝑖𝑑∧u.c-ids=∅u.S=\emptyset\implies u.\mathit{flyID}=u.\mathit{id}\land u.\textit{c-ids}=\emptyset.

  2. 2.

    u.L=∅∧u.R≠∅⟹u.𝑣𝐼𝐷=1∧u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=u.𝑖𝑑∧u.c-dist=0u.L=\emptyset\land u.R\neq\emptyset\implies u.\mathit{vID}=1\land u.\mathit{flyID}=u.\mathit{id}\land u.\textit{c-dist}=0.

  3. 3.

    u.L≠∅⟹u.c-dist>0∧u.vID>1u.L\neq\emptyset\implies u.\textit{c-dist}>0\land u.\textit{vID}>1.

  4. 4.

In that scheme, each node is given a “certificate” consisting of the root node id, a parent node id (among its neighbors) and the distance from the root (in a rooted spanning tree), where the “root” is the (only) node with its distance equal to 0 (and has no parent). Then, each node examines the certificates of its neighbors in the graph, and checks the distance (i.e., from its parent) and the root ids (i.e., whether they are same). If any certificate is incorrectly assigned, then there exists (at least) one node that “rejects” its certificate. Otherwise, if each certificate is correctly assigned (with respect to some rooted spanning tree), then each node “accepts” its certificate.

We use proof by contradiction to show that G′G^{\prime} is indeed G∗G^{*}. First, there cannot be a cycle in G′G^{\prime}, as the distance checks (i.e., from a node uu to its parent p⁡(u)p(u)) cannot be satisfied at all nodes (cf. Section 2.3). Moreover, G′G^{\prime} cannot be a spanning forest because all the nodes, via flyover id, can verify that there is only one “root node,” i.e., node v1v_{1} with distance v1.c-dist=0v_{1}.\textit{c-dist}=0. Thus, G′G^{\prime} forms a spanning tree. Combining the second invariant mentioned earlier, i.e., each node has degree at most 2, the tree must be a path. Finally, that path has to be the sorted-path G∗G^{*} due to the second invariant because every node checks that its locally sorted with its neighbors in G′G^{\prime}. ∎

C.4 Connectivity Preservation

Lemma C.21.

If the initial communication graph is weakly connected, then the communication graph in any round r≥1r\geq 1 is also weakly connected.

Proof.

Consider a node id vv in some node uu (whether in its channel or address variables, i.e., vv is present in a message sent to uu, or vv is assigned to some variable in uu). If vv is present in uu, then uu and vv are (weakly) connected. On the other hand, if vv is “delegated,” i.e., uu sends the id of vv to another node ww, then we need to show that uu and vv are (weakly) connected via some path (u,v1,…,vt)(u,v_{1},\dots,v_{t}) where vt=vv_{t}=v for some t≥1t\geq 1. Thus, we focus on all the possible cases in our algorithms where a node id could be delegated, and a node id is present in a received message, to show that the network remains weakly connected in the next round.

  • •

    First, by design, every node runs an algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} (in parallel, for converging to target topology) that preserves connectivity (i.e., following the universal overlay primitives for edge manipulations). Moreover, if nodes use the DR primitive (instead of “Delegate” primitive) while running algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}, connectivity is still preserved (as the direction of delegated edge is only opposite to the intended direction, but is subsequently reversed; see Definition C.7) after edge manipulations by algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} in any round.

  • •

    In the 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧,𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverConstruction},\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} and 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐂𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{TestConnCertificate} functions, if node uu sends vv to some other node, then vv also remains in node uu.

  • •

    We analyze the response functions that process the received messages.

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverConstruction} function, node uu processes two types of messages. For any message ⟨𝑚𝑠𝑔,𝑠𝑒𝑛⟩\langle\mathit{msg},\mathit{sen}\rangle, 𝑠𝑒𝑛\mathit{sen} is stored in, either u.Su.S or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}). For any message ⟨𝑚𝑠𝑔,w,i,𝑠𝑒𝑛⟩\langle\mathit{msg},w,i,\mathit{sen}\rangle, ww and 𝑠𝑒𝑛\mathit{sen} are stored in either u.Su.S or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverMetadata} function, for any message ⟨TestFlyID,𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID},\mathit{flyID}\rangle, there are two cases: 𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷\mathit{flyID} is stored in either u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐂𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{R\_TestConnCertificate} function, for any message ⟨TestCert,w,𝑣𝐼𝐷,𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡⟩\langle\text{TestCert},w,\mathit{vID},\mathit{dist}\rangle, there are three cases: (1) ww is sent to node u′∈u.Su^{\prime}\in u.S, in which case, there is a path (u,u′,w)(u,u^{\prime},w), or (2) uu stores ww in u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids}, or (3) uu stores ww in Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}); for any message ⟨IntroCert,w⟩\langle\text{IntroCert},w\rangle, uu stores ww in u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids}.

In 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐡\mathbf{JoinPath} function, for any message ⟨𝑚𝑠𝑔,v⟩\langle\mathit{msg},v\rangle, there are two cases: node uu stores vv either in u.Su.S or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

For any i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1], if all nodes in BsB_{s} have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 00 in rounds r,…,r+i′r,\dots,r+i^{\prime} where i′≥ii^{\prime}\geq i, then in any round r+i′r+i^{\prime}, the statements hold true, independently, for Bs1B^{1}_{s} and Bs2B^{2}_{s}, which implies, in round r+k−1r+k-1, u1.Sr​(k)=us′u_{1}.S_{r}(k)=u_{s^{\prime}} and us′.Sl​(k)=u1u_{s^{\prime}}.S_{l}(k)=u_{1} and us.Sl​(k)=us′u_{s}.S_{l}(k)=u_{s^{\prime}} and us′.Sr​(k)=usu_{s^{\prime}}.S_{r}(k)=u_{s}. In round r+k−1r+k-1, node us′u_{s^{\prime}} sends ⟨FlyConst-R,u1,k,us′⟩\langle\text{FlyConst-R},u_{1},k,u_{s^{\prime}}\rangle and ⟨FlyConst-L,us,k,us′⟩\langle\text{FlyConst-L},u_{s},k,u_{s^{\prime}}\rangle messages to node usu_{s} and u1u_{1} respectively. Since the nodes do not set their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variables to 11 in rounds r+k−1r+k-1 and r+kr+k, node u1u_{1} assigns usu_{s} to u1.Sr​(k+1)u_{1}.S_{r}(k+1) and node usu_{s} assigns u1u_{1} to us.Sl​(k+1)u_{s}.S_{l}(k+1) in round r+kr+k (if they have not already done so), which implies that |u1.R|≥k+1|u_{1}.R|\geq k+1 and |u3.L|≥k+1|u_{3}.L|\geq k+1 in round r+kr+k.
