Corollary C.23.

Consider any backbone BB in any round rr. If all nodes in BB have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 00 in all rounds r,r+1,…,r+ir,r+1,\dots,r+i where i≥⌊log2⁡(|B|−1)⌋i\geq\lfloor\log_{2}(|B|-1)\rfloor, then in any round r+ir+i, BB is a flyover.

C.6 Fast Information Dissemination

Lemma C.24.

Consider any backbone BB in any round rr. If there exists a node u∈Bu\in B such that u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1u.\mathit{exit}=1 at round rr, then by round r+2​⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+2\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor, all nodes in BB would’ve exited from the dual-state (at least once).

Proof.

Let dB​(p,q)d_{B}(p,q) denote the distance between any two nodes {p,q}⊆B\{p,q\}\subseteq B over the backbone BB in round rr. We recursively define it in the following way. (Note that this distance remains same, throughout the execution, as it is defined for backbone BB at round rr.)

dB​(p,q)={0if p=q,(dB(p.Sl(1),q))+1if (q.L=∅∨q.Sl(1)∉B),dB(p,q.Sl(1))+1if (p.L=∅∨p.Sl(1)∉B),|dB(p,r)−(dB(q,r)|otherwise, where r∈B∧(r.L=∅∨r.Sl(1)∉B).d_{B}(p,q)=\begin{cases}0&\text{if $p=q$},\\ (d_{B}(p.S_{l}(1),q))+1&\text{if $(q.L=\emptyset\lor q.S_{l}(1)\notin B)$},\\ d_{B}(p,q.S_{l}(1))+1&\text{if $(p.L=\emptyset\lor p.S_{l}(1)\notin B)$},\\ \lvert d_{B}(p,r)-(d_{B}(q,r)\rvert&\text{otherwise, where $r\in B\land(r.L=\emptyset\lor r.S_{l}(1)\notin B)$}.\end{cases}

Let DB​(v)=minw∈B∧w.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1⁡dB​(w,v)D_{B}(v)=\min_{w\in B\land w.\mathit{exit}=1}d_{B}(w,v) denote the minimum distance, over all nodes in BB that have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 1, to the node v∈Bv\in B.

If at round r′∈{r,…,r+2​⌊log⁡|B|⌋−1}r^{\prime}\in\{r,\dots,r+2\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor-1\}, if either (v.L≠∅∧v.Sl(1)∈B∧v.Sl(1).𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1)(v.L\neq\emptyset\land v.S_{l}(1)\in B\land v.S_{l}(1).\mathit{exit}=1) or (v.R≠∅∧v.Sr(1)∈B∧v.Sr(1).𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1)(v.R\neq\emptyset\land v.S_{r}(1)\in B\land v.S_{r}(1).\mathit{exit}=1), i.e., DB​(v)<2D_{B}(v)<2, then node vv exits the dual-state in round r′+1r^{\prime}+1. This is due to Remark C.17, every node, in 𝐅𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{FlushFlyover} function, sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to all ids in its flyover-related address variables. Moreover, if DB​(v)≥2D_{B}(v)\geq 2 in round rr, then we show that it decreases exponentially over time (due to flyover construction, i.e., pointer doubling [46]).

Consider a backbone Bk={v1,k,v2,k,…}B_{k}=\{v_{1,k},v_{2,k},\dots\} in round r+kr+k, where (v1,k.L=∅∨v1,k.Sl(1)∉Bk)(v_{1,k}.L=\emptyset\lor v_{1,k}.S_{l}(1)\notin B_{k}) and ∀i∈[|Bk|−1],vi,k.Sr​(1)=vi+1,k\forall i\in[|B_{k}|-1],v_{i,k}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1,k}, and B0=BB_{0}=B. In round r+kr+k, consider a node ww that satisfies dB​(w,v)=DB​(v)≥2d_{B}(w,v)=D_{B}(v)\geq 2, and the backbone Bk={v1,k,…,v|Bk|,k}B_{k}=\{v_{1,k},\dots,v_{|B_{k}|,k}\}, part of the original backbone BB, such that either (v1,k=w∧v|Bk|,k=v)(v_{1,k}=w\land v_{|B_{k}|,k}=v) or (v1,k=v∧v|Bk|,k=w)(v_{1,k}=v\land v_{|B_{k}|,k}=w) is true. For any k≥1k\geq 1, by Lemma C.22, we know that ∀j∈[k],v1,k.Sr​(j)=v1+2j,k\forall j\in[k],v_{1,k}.S_{r}(j)=v_{1+2^{j},k} and ∀j∈[k],v|Bk|,k.Sl​(j)=v|Bk|−2j,k\forall j\in[k],v_{|B_{k}|,k}.S_{l}(j)=v_{|B_{k}|-2^{j},k}. Thus, by round r+2​⌊log⁡|B|⌋−1r+2\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor-1, either node vv exited the dual-state, or DB​(v)<2D_{B}(v)<2. ∎

C.7 Concurrent Advices

Claim C.25.

Consider any set of nodes Q⊂VQ\subset V that process advice messages in round rr. For any node v∈Qv\in Q, if the advice is effective, then for any node u∉Qu\notin Q, then u∉v.Su\notin v.S after vv enters dual-state.

Proof.

Once any node receives an advice, if the node id present in it, is also part of its memory (i.e., in snap variable), then the node proceeds to check that the distance (i.e., in dist variable) matches with its “parent” node id (as in the advice). See Algorithm 12 for more details. This back-and-forth verification of advice between a node and its parent in a synchronous system, before executing the tree-to-path transformation (i.e., Algorithm 13), ensures that they must have processed the advice in the same round. If any node u∉Qu\notin Q is not part of this back-and-forth communication, then it is not part of 𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐩𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦\mathbf{SetupLocalTransform} function in Algorithm 12, which in turn, implies that it is also not part of 𝐋𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦\mathbf{LocalTransform} and 𝐉𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐡\mathbf{JoinPath} functions in Algorithm 13. Thus, ∀v∈Q,u∉v.S\forall v\in Q,u\notin v.S. ∎

Lemma C.26.

Let DD be the set of nodes in dual-state in any round r>5r>5. Let D′D^{\prime} be the set of nodes that transition to dual-state in round r+1r+1. For any pair of nodes u∈Du\in D and v∈D′v\in D^{\prime}, u∉v.Su\notin v.S in round r+1r+1.

Proof.

Consider the following (exhaustive) cases for any node u∈Du\in D in round rr.

  1. 1.

    Node uu was always in dual-state from round 1.

  2. 2.

    Node uu processed an advice message in a round r′≤r−3r^{\prime}\leq r-3, as the distributed tree-to-path algorithms (cf. Section A.2.2) takes 3 rounds, until node uu enters dual-state.

Each node in D′D^{\prime}, as it enters dual-state in round r+1r+1, processed an advice message at round r−2r-2. Let QQ be the set of nodes that processed advice messages in round r−2r-2. Clearly, u∉Qu\notin Q (as u.t≠0u.t\neq 0 or u.S≠∅u.S\neq\emptyset in that round). Thus, by Claim C.25, any pair of nodes u∈Du\in D and v∈D′v\in D^{\prime}, u∉v.Su\notin v.S. ∎

C.8 Fast Detection of Bad Advice

Lemma C.27.

Let B={v1,…,v|B|}B=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{|B|}\} be a maximal backbone in round r>5r>5, where either (v1.Sl(1)∉B)(v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\notin B) or (v|B|.Sr(1)∉B)(v_{|B|}.S_{r}(1)\notin B) is satisfied. Let LL be the set of lost nodes in round rr. There is at least node in BB that sets its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1 by round r+2r+2. Moreover, every node in LL sets its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1 by round r+2r+2.

Proof.

We provide the proof for the backbone BB, but the same argument applies to the lost nodes in LL. Wlog, let node v1.L≠∅v_{1}.L\neq\emptyset; similar argument also applies to v|B|v_{|B|} if v|B|.R≠∅v_{|B|}.R\neq\emptyset.

Node v1v_{1} sends ⟨TestLine-L⟩\langle\text{TestLine-L}\rangle to v1.Sl​(1)v_{1}.S_{l}(1) in round rr. But v1.Sl​(1)v_{1}.S_{l}(1), in round r+1r+1, by Lemma C.26, as it holds that (v1.Sl(1)).Sr(1)≠v1(v_{1}.S_{l}(1)).S_{r}(1)\neq v_{1}, sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to v1v_{1} (regardless whether v1.Sl​(1)v_{1}.S_{l}(1) in a dual-state or not). Node v1v_{1} its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 1 by round r+2r+2. ∎

Lemma C.28.

Each node in a maximal ouroboros OO in round r>5r>5, exits dual-state in O⁡(log⁡|O|)O(\log|O|) rounds.

Proof.

By Lemma C.26, the size of any maximal ouroboros (or maximal backbone) doesn’t increase over time (i.e., for any round r′>rr^{\prime}>r, if some node u∉Ou\notin O, then u∉Ou\notin O in round r′r^{\prime}). Let us consider the two cases of maximal ouroboros (as in Definition C.10) in round rr.

  1. 1.

    If OO is a perfect ring, then at least one pair of consecutive nodes in OO set their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variables to 1 by round r+1r+1, as by design, every node uu in its dual-state, uu sends u.𝑣𝐼𝐷+1u.\mathit{vID}+1 to u.Sr​(1)u.S_{r}(1) and u.𝑣𝐼𝐷−1u.\mathit{vID}-1 to u.Sl​(1)u.S_{l}(1) in every round. Let L⊆OL\subseteq O be the set of nodes that are lost in round r+2r+2; they exit from dual-state by round r+4r+4 by Lemma C.27. The set of nodes O′⊆(O∖L)O^{\prime}\subseteq(O\setminus L), that are in dual-state but not lost in round r+2r+2, forms a partition of maximal winged backbones as every node u∈Ou\in O in round rr, has u.L≠∅∧u.R≠∅u.L\neq\emptyset\land u.R\neq\emptyset. By Lemma C.27, combined with Lemma C.24, by round r+O⁡(log⁡|O|)r+O(\log|O|), all nodes in O′O^{\prime} exit the dual-state.

  2. 2.

    If OO is a stylish ring, then there is at least one node u∈Ou\in O such that,

    {u.Sl(1),u.Sr(1)}⊆O∧((v=u.Sl(1)∧v.Sr(1)≠u)∨(v=u.Sr(1)∧v.Sl(1)≠u)).\{u.S_{l}(1),u.S_{r}(1)\}\subseteq O\land((v=u.S_{l}(1)\land v.S_{r}(1)\neq u)\lor(v=u.S_{r}(1)\land v.S_{l}(1)\neq u)).

    Node uu sends ⟨TestLine-R⟩\langle\text{TestLine-R}\rangle and ⟨TestLine-L⟩\langle\text{TestLine-L}\rangle messages in round rr. In round r+1r+1, (at least) one of the recipients, sets the 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1, and sends back ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to node uu. By round r+2r+2, node uu exits the dual-state. Let L⊆OL\subseteq O be the set of nodes that are lost in round r+2r+2; they exit from dual-state by round r+4r+4 by Lemma C.27. The set of nodes O′⊆O∖(M∪L)O^{\prime}\subseteq O\setminus(M\cup L) that are in dual-state but not lost in round r+2r+2, form a partition of maximal winged backbones, as every node v∈O′v\in O^{\prime} in round rr, has v.L≠∅∧v.R≠∅v.L\neq\emptyset\land v.R\neq\emptyset. By Lemma C.27 and Lemma C.24, by round r+O⁡(log⁡|O|)r+O(\log|O|), all nodes in O′O^{\prime} exit the dual-state.

∎

Lemma C.29.

Consider any maximal backbone B⊆VB\subseteq V in any round r>5r>5, where BB is not winged. If all nodes in BB have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 00 in all rounds r,r+1,…,Tr,r+1,\dots,T, then the following statements hold.

  1. 1.

    If T≥r+2​⌈log⁡|B|⌉T\geq r+2\lceil\log|B|\rceil, then in any round r′∈{r+2​⌈log⁡|B|⌉,…,T}r^{\prime}\in\{r+2\lceil\log|B|\rceil,\dots,T\}, BB is a flyover, and for all u∈B,u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=v.𝑖𝑑u\in B,u.\mathit{flyID}=v.\mathit{id} where v.L=∅v.L=\emptyset.

  2. 2.

    If T≥r+3​⌈log⁡|B|⌉T\geq r+3\lceil\log|B|\rceil, and for all u∈B,u.S⊆Bu\in B,u.S\subseteq B, then in any round r′∈{r+3​⌈log⁡|B|⌉,…,T}r^{\prime}\in\{r+3\lceil\log|B|\rceil,\dots,T\}, backbone BB is correctly configured.

Proof.

First, by Lemma C.26, the size of any maximal backbone doesn’t increase over time (i.e., for any round r′≥rr^{\prime}\geq r, if some node v∉Bv\notin B in round rr, then v∉Bv\notin B in round r′r^{\prime}). Since BB is not a winged maximal backbone, i.e., there exist v1v_{1} and v|B|v_{|B|} nodes in BB such that (v1.L=∅)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset) and (v|B|.R=∅)(v_{|B|}.R=\emptyset).

Due to our algorithm design, we recall the possible changes of flyover-related variables for any node uu whose u.S≠∅u.S\neq\emptyset and u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=0u.\mathit{exit}=0.

  1. 1.

    The variables vID,c-par,c-dist\texttt{vID},\texttt{c-par},\texttt{c-dist} are initially updated after receiving an advice message from the supervisor (see 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞\mathbf{GetAdvice} function). But they can only be updated again once the node executes 𝐅𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{FlushFlyover} function (i.e., after u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1u.\mathit{exit}=1).

  2. 2.

    If u.L=∅∧u.R≠∅u.L=\emptyset\land u.R\neq\emptyset, then u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=u.𝑖𝑑u.\mathit{flyID}=u.\mathit{id}; otherwise, the variable flyID can be assigned some other id in 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverMetadata} function. Importantly, once u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷≠u.𝑖𝑑u.\mathit{flyID}\neq u.\mathit{id}, it can only be updated again once the node executes 𝐅𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{FlushFlyover} function (i.e., after u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1u.\mathit{exit}=1).

  3. 3.

    The variables L,R\texttt{L},\texttt{R} and c-ids can be updated over time in that the existing ids in the variables cannot be removed but new ids can be added. Thus, this means that u.Sl​(1)u.S_{l}(1) and u.Sr​(1)u.S_{r}(1) can be updated again once the node executes 𝐅𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫\mathbf{FlushFlyover} function (i.e., after u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=1u.\mathit{exit}=1).

As all nodes have their exit variable set to 0, let us go over the required variable changes of a correctly configured flyover (as in Definitions C.12 and C.13). Wlog, let B={v1,v2,…,v|B|}B=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{|B|}\}. If the following events do not happen, then ∃v∈B,v.𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝=1\exists v\in B,v.\mathtt{exit}=1 by round r+3​⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+3\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor.

  1. 1.

    (Virtual IDs) As v1.L=∅v_{1}.L=\emptyset, v1.𝑣𝐼𝐷v_{1}.\mathit{vID} must be equal to 1. For all i∈[|B|]i\in[|B|], in round r+1r+1, due to the 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} function, viv_{i} must be equal to ii.

  2. 2.

    (Hypercube Edges) By Lemma C.22 (and Corollary C.23), by round r+⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor, backbone BB is a flyover (as per Definition C.12) due to the 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧\mathbf{TestFlyoverConstruction} function.

  3. 3.

    (Flyover ID) By round r+2​⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+2\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor, for all i∈[|B|]i\in[|B|], vi.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷v_{i}.\mathit{flyID} must be equal to v1v_{1} due to the 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} function (as BB must be a flyover by round r+⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor).

  4. 4.

    (Connectivity Certificate) At round r+2​⌊log⁡|B|⌋r+2\lfloor\log|B|\rfloor, the prop-flyID variable is set to 1 for any node u∈Bu\in B, as the clause (u.𝑣𝐼𝐷=1)∨(u.𝑣𝐼𝐷>1∧u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=v1)(u.\mathit{vID}=1)\lor(u.\mathit{vID}>1\land u.\mathit{flyID}=v_{1}) is satisfied. For all i∈[|B|]∖{1}i\in[|B|]\setminus\{1\}, node viv_{i} routes the vi.c-dist−1v_{i}.\textit{c-dist}-1 value (over the flyover) to the node with the virtual ID vi.c-parv_{i}.\textit{c-par} using the 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐩\mathbf{NextStop} function. The message must be routed to some node within the flyover, and that node verifies the message with its c-dist variable. Combined with the tests in the 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤𝐬\mathbf{BasicChecks} function, this results in adding the appropriate neighboring ids in the sorted-path graph over backbone BB (as per Definition C.13) by the next ⌈log⁡|B|⌉\lceil\log|B|\rceil rounds.

∎

Corollary C.30.

Let all nodes form a single backbone in round rr. If all nodes have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 0 in all rounds r,r+1,…,r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉r,r+1,\dots,r+3\lceil\log n\rceil, then the (sub)network over ∀u∈V,Mu​(𝒜0)\forall u\in V,\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}), includes the sorted-path topology in round r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉r+3\lceil\log n\rceil.

Lemma C.31.

Consider a maximal backbone B={v1,…,v|B|}B=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{|B|}\} in any round r>5r>5, where |B|<n|B|<n and (v1.L=∅∨v1.Sl(1)∉B)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset\lor v_{1}.S_{l}(1)\notin B) and ∀i∈[|B|−1],vi.Sr​(1)=vi+1\forall i\in[|B|-1],v_{i}.S_{r}(1)=v_{i+1}. By round r+O⁡(log⁡n)r+O(\log n), at least one node in BB will set its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1.

Proof.

First, by Lemma C.26, the size of any maximal backbone doesn’t increase over time (i.e., for any round r′>rr^{\prime}>r, if some node u∉Bu\notin B, then u∉Bu\notin B in round r′r^{\prime}).

If BB is a maximal winged backbone in round rr, then by Lemma C.27, at least one node in BB sets its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable set to 1 by round r+2r+2. Thus, for the rest of the proof, we consider the scenario where BB is not a winged maximal backbone, i.e., (v1.L=∅)(v_{1}.L=\emptyset) and (v|B|.R=∅)(v_{|B|}.R=\emptyset).

Furthermore, for the rest of the proof, we consider the scenario where, no node in BB sets its exit variable to 1 by round r+2​⌈log⁡n⌉r+2\lceil\log n\rceil. (Otherwise, that would only support the lemma statement.) By Lemma C.29, in any round r′≥r+2​⌈log⁡n⌉r^{\prime}\geq r+2\lceil\log n\rceil, BB is a flyover, and ∀u∈B,u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=v1\forall u\in B,u.\mathit{flyID}=v_{1}.

Recall that the communication graph is weakly connected in any round (due to Lemma C.21). We split the proof into multiple cases (and subcases), analyzing how the backbone BB gets affected from the existence of a directed edge (p,q)(p,q) in round r′r^{\prime}, where (p∈B∧q∉B)(p\in B\land q\notin B) or (p∉B∧q∈B)(p\notin B\land q\in B).

  2. 2.

By Lemma C.27 and Lemma C.28, qq exits the dual-state by round r′+O⁡(log⁡n)r^{\prime}+O(\log n), and sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to all ids in q.S∪{q.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷}∪q.c-idsq.S\cup\{q.\mathit{flyID}\}\cup q.\textit{c-ids}.

Clearly, Bq∩B=∅B_{q}\cap B=\emptyset (as both are maximal), so p.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷∉Bqp.\mathit{flyID}\notin B_{q} and q′∉Bq^{\prime}\notin B. If some node in BqB_{q} exits dual-state by round r′+2​⌈log⁡n⌉r^{\prime}+2\lceil\log n\rceil, then by Lemma C.24, qq exits the dual-state by round r′+4​⌈log⁡n⌉r^{\prime}+4\lceil\log n\rceil and sends ⟨RejFlyover⟩\langle\text{RejFlyover}\rangle to all ids in q.S∪{q.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷}∪q.c-idsq.S\cup\{q.\mathit{flyID}\}\cup q.\textit{c-ids}. On the other hand, if no node in BqB_{q} sets its exit variable to 1 until round r′+2​⌈log⁡n⌉r^{\prime}+2\lceil\log n\rceil, then by Lemma C.29, the prop-flyID variable is set to 1 in qq, after which q′=q.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷q^{\prime}=q.\mathit{flyID} is sent to pp, due to 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} function, causing pp to set its exit variable to 1, as p.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷≠q.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷p.\mathit{flyID}\neq q.\mathit{flyID}.

Node id qq is stored in (memory or channel of) pp. As all nodes in BB have their prop-flyID variable set to 1, node qq receives ⟨TestFlyID,p.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID},p.\mathit{flyID}\rangle in round r′+1r^{\prime}+1. When q.t≤1q.t\leq 1, q.𝑣𝐼𝐷q.\mathit{vID} is set to 0, causing node qq to send ⟨TestFlyID,⊥⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID},\bot\rangle to all ids in 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} function (before qq processes a new advice message; see Remark C.18). In that round, node qq sends ⟨TestFlyID,⊥⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID},\bot\rangle to all ids in 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{TestFlyoverMetadata} function (before qq processes a new advice message; see Remark C.18), causing pp to set its exit variable to 1.

C.9 Putting Everything Together

Claim C.32.

If a node is in a precarious dual-state in round rr, it exits dual-state by round r+O⁡(log⁡n)r+O(\log n).

Proof.

For the first three cases of the precarious dual-state property (see Definition C.14), if all nodes do not form a single backbone, then by Lemma C.27, Lemma C.28 and Lemma C.31, combined with fast information dissemination (i.e., Lemma C.24), every node exits the dual-state in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. However, if the network forms a single backbone, and if some node is sets its exit variable to 1 by round r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉r+3\lceil\log n\rceil, then again, combined with Lemma C.24, every node exits the dual-state by round r+O⁡(log⁡n)r+O(\log n). ∎

Theorem C.33.

The network is s-robust.

Proof.

By design (see, 𝐆𝐞𝐭𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞\mathbf{GetAdvice} function in Algorithm 12, and Definition C.4 for “well-formed” advice), for any node uu, (1) there can be only one node id present in any advice message, and (2) that id must already be present in the 𝚜𝚗𝚊𝚙\mathtt{snap} variable when the advice is received at node uu. Thus, the supervisor cannot add arbitrary connections to any node, ensuring the Sybil resistance property.

If any node is in a precarious dual-state (see Definition C.14), then by Claim C.32, it exits the dual-state in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. On the other hand, if no node is in a precarious dual-state, and the network forms a single backbone, and no node sets its exit variable to 1 for Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) rounds, then by Lemma C.29, the backbone is a correctly configured flyover (i.e., the supervisor provided correct advice messages), i.e., by Corollary C.30, the network is in an almost-legal configuration. Moreover, this observation implies that even if the supervisor is malicious (e.g., providing “bad” advice messages), the network quickly rejects the “supervised-induced” subnetwork (from any arbitrary configuration). Thus, the network also achieves the robustness property, which would allow an honest supervisor to quickly (i.e., in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds) contact all nodes, provide correct advice messages to repair the network. ∎

Claim C.34.

Consider a node id vv in any flyover-related or advice-related message of a node uu in round rr. By round r+1r+1, one of the following events happen, where w=u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷w=u.\mathit{flyID} in round rr.

  1. 1.

    v∈u.S∪{u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷}∪u.c-idsv\in u.S\cup\{u.\mathit{flyID}\}\cup u.\textit{c-ids}.

  2. 2.

    v∈Mu​(𝒜0)v\in\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

  3. 3.

    v.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷=wv.\mathit{flyID}=w.

  4. 4.

    w∈Mv​(𝒜0)w\in\mathrm{M}_{v}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

Proof.

Similar to the proof of Lemma C.21, we provide a case-by-case analysis depending on the message that the node id vv is part of.

  1. 1.

    If u.S=∅u.S=\emptyset, in functions, 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧,𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverConstruction},\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverMetadata} and 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐂𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{R\_TestConnCertificate}, node id vv straightaway gets added to Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) in round rr.

  2. 2.

    If vv belongs to any function in the distributed tree-to-path algorithms (cf. Section A.2.2), again, node id vv straightaway gets added to Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) in round rr.

  3. 3.

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverConstruction} function, node uu processes two types of messages. For any message ⟨𝑚𝑠𝑔,𝑠𝑒𝑛⟩\langle\mathit{msg},\mathit{sen}\rangle, 𝑠𝑒𝑛\mathit{sen} is stored in, either u.Su.S or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}). For any message ⟨𝑚𝑠𝑔,w,i,𝑠𝑒𝑛⟩\langle\mathit{msg},w,i,\mathit{sen}\rangle, ww and 𝑠𝑒𝑛\mathit{sen} are stored in either u.Su.S or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐅𝐥𝐲𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚\mathbf{R\_TestFlyoverMetadata} function, for any message ⟨TestFlyID,𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷⟩\langle\text{TestFlyID},\mathit{flyID}\rangle, there are two cases: 𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷\mathit{flyID} is stored in either u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷u.\mathit{flyID} or Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

  4. 4.

    In 𝐑​_​𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐂𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞\mathbf{R\_TestConnCertificate} function, for any message ⟨TestCert,v,𝑣𝐼𝐷,𝑑𝑖𝑠𝑡⟩\langle\text{TestCert},v,\mathit{vID},\mathit{dist}\rangle, there are three cases: (1) vv is sent to node u′∈u.Su^{\prime}\in u.S, or (2) uu stores vv in u.c-idsu.\textit{c-ids}, or (3) uu stores vv in Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}); in the first case, before vv is sent to an id u′∈u.Su^{\prime}\in u.S, uu must’ve sent ⟨TestFlyID,u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷⟩\langle\mathrm{TestFlyID},u.\mathit{flyID}\rangle to vv in round rr (as the prop-flyID variable is set to 1). Theorem C.35.

If supervisor is honest, then the network reaches an almost-legal configuration in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds; otherwise, it reaches an almost-legal configuration in 2​R​(𝒜0)+O⁡(log⁡n)2\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0})+O(\log n) rounds.

Proof.

We denote the subnetwork formed by edges in ∀u∈V,Mu​(𝒜0)\forall u\in V,\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) as N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}). Recall that the communication graph is always weakly connected (in any round) due to Lemma C.21.

First, we introduce some notation for showing that N⁡(𝒜0)N(\mathcal{A}_{0}) would be (weakly) connected. Let the (directed) edge (u,v)(u,v) in the communication graph in any round r≥1r\geq 1; we define the color of an edge (u,v)(u,v) in the following way.

  1. 1.

    If (v∉Mu(𝒜0))∧(v∉u.S∪{u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷}∪u.c-ids)(v\notin\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}))\land(v\notin u.S\cup\{u.\mathit{flyID}\}\cup u.\textit{c-ids}), but node id vv is present in a flyover-related or advice-related message in uu, then the color of (u,v)(u,v) is red.

  2. 2.

    If (v∉Mu(𝒜0))∧(v∈u.S∪{u.𝑓𝑙𝑦𝐼𝐷}∪u.c-ids)(v\notin\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}))\land(v\in u.S\cup\{u.\mathit{flyID}\}\cup u.\textit{c-ids}), then the color of (u,v)(u,v) is blue.

  3. 3.

    If v∈Mu​(𝒜0)v\in\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}), then the color of the edge (u,v)(u,v) is green. Similarly, we say that a path between any pair of nodes (ignoring edge directions) is a green path if all edges in it are green.

We proceed to show that N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) forms a single (weakly) connected component, i.e., there exists a green path between any pair of nodes, in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, regardless of the initial configuration and any node’s interactions with the supervisor. If N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) is weakly connected, then it always remains a single (weakly) connected component in any subsequent round, as Algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} is a self-stabilizing overlay algorithm (i.e., it preserves connectivity from any initial configuration), and importantly, nodes do not delete connections from the memory (incl. channel) dedicated to Algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} while interacting with the supervisor (cf. Theorem C.33).

Towards that end, consider any pair of nodes uu and vv that do not have any green path between them in any round r≥1r\geq 1. As the communication graph is weakly connected, there exists some (undirected, i.e., ignoring edge directions) path P=(u,v1,…,vt)P=(u,v_{1},\dots,v_{t}), where vt=vv_{t}=v for t≥1t\geq 1, in that round. Consider any edge e=(p,q)e=(p,q) belonging to PP; the following invariants hold in round r+1r+1.

  1. 1.

    If ee is red, then ee turns either blue or green, due to Claim C.34.

  2. 2.

    If ee is blue, then ee either remains blue or turns green, due to Remark C.17.

  3. 3.

    If ee is green, then due to the guarantee that Algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} preserves connectivity, there exists some green path Pe=(p,q1,…,qt′)P_{e}=(p,q_{1},\dots,q_{t^{\prime}}), where qt′=qq_{t^{\prime}}=q for t′≥1t^{\prime}\geq 1.

We proceed to show that any blue edge turns green in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. Consider any blue edge e=(p,q)e=(p,q), where the node id qq belongs to a flyover-related address variable of node pp. In the following (exhaustive) cases, nodes pp and qq end up with a green path between them.

  1. 1.

    If p.S=∅p.S=\emptyset, then all flyover-related address variables of pp are straightaway flushed to Mp​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{p}(\mathcal{A}_{0}).

  2. 2.

    If pp is in a precarious dual-state, then by Claim C.32, pp exits dual-state in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

  3. 3.

    If the network forms a single backbone, and if all nodes have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variables set to 0 in all rounds r,r+1,…,r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉r,r+1,\dots,r+3\lceil\log n\rceil. By Corollary C.30, N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) becomes (weakly) connected.

If N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) is (weakly) connected (regardless of any supervisor interaction), the network reaches an almost-legal configuration in 2​R​(𝒜0)2\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) rounds. This is because each node uu executes Algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0} (in the background), and it is guaranteed that Algorithm 𝒜0\mathcal{A}_{0}, when executed independently, converges to the target topology G∗G^{*} in R⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) rounds. There is an extra factor of 2, in our upper bound, because “Delegation” (of a node id by any node via a message), that takes a single round, is implemented in two rounds as “Delegate-after-Reversal” (see Definition C.7). Thus, if supervisor is not honest, the network reaches an almost-legal configuration in 2​R​(𝒜0)+O⁡(log⁡n)2\mathrm{R}(\mathcal{A}_{0})+O(\log n) rounds.

If the supervisor is honest, we can leverage the (correct) advice for showing fast stabilization. First, we show that within O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, there exists at least one attentive node, in which case, the supervisor is contacted for help. Once the supervisor is contacted by a node, the supervisor waits for O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds until all nodes become attentive. Then, the supervisor sends the correct advice messages, leading to all nodes forming a correctly-configured flyover in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. Finally, each node finds its predecessor and successor (in the sorted-path topology G∗G^{*}) in the c-id variable, due to Corollary C.30, as no node sets its 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variable to 1.

Towards that end, we prove the following arguments.

  1. 1.

    If N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) does not include G∗G^{*} in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, then there exists at least one attentive node in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds. (If G∗G^{*} is already included, then we are done.)

  2. 2.

    If there is one attentive node, then all nodes become attentive in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

Consider the following (exhaustive) cases in any round r>5r>5.

  1. 1.

    By Claim C.32, any node in a precarious dual-state exits dual-state in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds.

  2. 2.

    If the network forms a single backbone, and if all nodes have their 𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝\mathtt{exit} variables set to 0 in all rounds r,r+1,…,r+3​⌈log⁡n⌉r,r+1,\dots,r+3\lceil\log n\rceil. By Corollary C.30, N⁡(𝒜0)\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{A}_{0}) becomes (weakly) connected.

For any node uu, u.tu.t decreases by one in every round (and u.tu.t can be at most 55). (See 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐜𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤𝐬𝟐\mathbf{BasicChecks2} function in Section A.2.2). By Claim C.34, if there is any node id vv in any flyover-related or advice-related message of any node uu (where u.S=∅u.S=\emptyset), then it is flushed to Mu​(𝒜0)\mathrm{M}_{u}(\mathcal{A}_{0}). Once node uu exits dual-state, it becomes attentive (i.e., u.S=∧u.𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡=0∧u.t=0u.S=\land u.\mathit{exit}=0\land u.t=0) in O⁡(1)O(1) rounds. Thus, either all nodes become attentive in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, or N⁡(𝒜0)N(\mathcal{A}_{0}) includes the target topology G∗G^{*}. ∎

C.10 Lower Bound for Convergence Time

Theorem C.36.

For an s-robust network, there exists some initial configuration such that the convergence time for any pair of supervisor and overlay algorithms is Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) rounds.

Proof.

Consider an initial configuration where two nodes uu and vv are at a distance D=Ω⁡(n)D=\Omega(n) in the communication graph. However, these nodes are meant to be adjacent in target topology G∗G^{*}. If there is a pair of supervisor and self-stabilizing overlay algorithm for which this network reaches an almost-legal configuration in o⁡(log⁡D)o(\log D) rounds, then we can show a contradiction that the nodes uu and vv were at a distance d<Dd<D in the initial state.

Recall that the nodes of an s-robust network do not arbitrarily create connections of any node id present in the advice message. In particular, a node can only add (directed) edges between any two ids present in its memory or channel. Thus, even if the supervisor is aware of memory states (incl. channels) of all nodes, and is allowed to interact with any subsets of nodes simultaneously, it is still limited in its power to create new connections.

Let tt be the minimum number of rounds (from that initial configuration at round 11) taken for node uu to acquire the id of node vv (or vice versa) in its channel. Let S=(a1,a2,…,at=u)S=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{t}=u) be the sequence of nodes from round 11 to tt holding the id of vv (until it reached uu). For ease of exposition, let us consider the class of distributed overlay algorithms that only add new (directed) edges, i.e, do not remove existing edges. If we arrive at a contradiction for this class of algorithms, then it also applies to all other algorithms.

To that end, observe that for this class of algorithms, the ids in SS must initially belong to some path PP (regardless of directions) from vv to uu. The key observation is that for i∈[t−1]i\in[t-1], between aia_{i} and ai+1a_{i+1} in the path PP, there can be at most 2i−1−12^{i-1}-1 nodes (and 2i−12^{i-1} edges), i.e., node ai+1a_{i+1} cannot be too far from node aia_{i} in the initial communication graph. This is because even if all nodes introduce all ids stored in their respective memories (incl. channels) to each other via messages in all rounds, each node can only learn all ids in its 2j2^{j}-hop neighborhood in jj rounds. Thus, the total number of edges (i.e., distance between vv and uu) in this path PP is at most 2t2^{t}.

Therefore, we arrive at a contradiction that if there exists a pair of supervisor and self-stabilizing overlay algorithm for which the network reached an almost-legal configuration in t=o⁡(log⁡D)t=o(\log D) rounds, then uu and vv must have been at a distance of at most 2t<D2^{t}<D in the initial configuration. ∎
